# payload-auth-link (full)

> payload-auth-link: a hexagonal ports/adapters Payload CMS auth plugin. Identity providers (Better Auth, Auth.js) are swappable adapters behind IdentityProviderPort; users stay first-class Payload documents. First-class Next.js (Payload v3) and TanStack Start (Payload v4) adapters share one framework-free web core. ESM-only, strict TypeScript, Result-based errors. Example apps at examples/basic and examples/tanstack-start; 24 Playwright specs green per suite across SQLite, Postgres, and Mongo on both frameworks (SQLite suites in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit).

---

<!-- docs/getting-started.md -->

# Getting started

Four edits take a Payload CMS v3 + Next.js site from zero to signed-in
users with Better Auth: install, engine, config, routes + UI. Every
snippet below is copied from `examples/basic`, which the e2e suite
exercises on SQLite, Postgres, and Mongo — if a snippet and the example
disagree, the example wins (and please file an issue).

Prerequisites: Bun 1.4+, a Payload 3 + Next.js 15+ app, React 19.
All packages are ESM-only (`type: module`, `engines: node >= 20.9`).

## Edit 1 — Install

```bash
bun add @payload-auth-link/core @payload-auth-link/plugin \
  @payload-auth-link/react @payload-auth-link/next \
  @payload-auth-link/provider-better-auth better-auth
```

(`better-auth` is a **peer dependency** of the provider since 0.3.0 —
validated band `>=1.7.6 <1.8.0` — and you import it yourself for the
`nextCookies()` framework plugin in Edit 2 anyway, so install it
directly.)

## Edit 2 — The engine (`lib/auth.ts`)

The engine composes Better Auth on Payload storage. `getPayload` is a
thunk (cached here) so the engine never imports your Payload config
statically — no import cycle.

```ts
import { createBetterAuthEngine } from '@payload-auth-link/provider-better-auth'
import { nextCookies } from 'better-auth/next-js'
import { getPayload, type Payload } from 'payload'

let cachedPayload: Promise<Payload> | undefined

function loadPayload(): Promise<Payload> {
  cachedPayload ??= import('../payload.config').then((mod) => getPayload({ config: mod.default }))
  return cachedPayload
}

export const engine = createBetterAuthEngine({
  getPayload: loadPayload,
  options: {
    baseURL: process.env.EXAMPLE_BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3100',
    secret: process.env.PAYLOAD_SECRET ?? 'local-dev-only-secret-32-chars-min!',
    // Framework cookie plugin, declared by you exactly as Better Auth
    // documents: required for cookie handling in Next.js server
    // actions. The engine never touches this list.
    plugins: [nextCookies()],
    emailAndPassword: {
      enabled: true,
      // Local example only: no email delivery here, so verification is
      // off. The engine requires verification by default — production
      // builders keep the default and configure an email sender.
      requireEmailVerification: false,
    },
  },
})

export const { auth, provider: betterAuthProvider, collections: betterAuthCollections } = engine
```

Notes:

- `options` is Better Auth's own options object, passed through
  verbatim except `database` (wired to Payload here). Your plugins,
  rate limits, and session settings keep working — and keep their
  types, since the engine's return type is inferred.
- With `emailAndPassword` present, the engine **requires email
  verification by default**. The snippet above opts out only because
  the example has no email delivery; production sites keep the
  default and configure a sender. Unverified users can hold provider
  sessions but the plugin refuses to link them to Payload users
  (see [Concepts](concepts.md)).
- Casing callout: the engine takes Better Auth's `baseURL` (capital
  URL) while the plugin takes Payload-style `baseUrl` (Edit 3).
  Each spelling belongs to its owner — do not "fix" either one.

## Edit 3 — The plugin (`payload.config.ts`)

```ts
import { authLink } from '@payload-auth-link/plugin'
import { betterAuthCollections, betterAuthProvider } from './lib/auth'

export default buildConfig({
  // …your db, secret, serverURL…
  collections: [
    { slug: 'users', auth: true, fields: [] },
    // …your collections…
    ...betterAuthCollections,
  ],
  plugins: [
    authLink({
      baseUrl: process.env.EXAMPLE_BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3100',
      roles: ['admin', 'user'],
      defaultRole: 'user',
      providers: [betterAuthProvider],
    }),
  ],
})
```

What this does:

- Appends the Better Auth system collections (`ba-users`,
  `ba-sessions`, `ba-accounts`, `ba-verifications`, `ba-rate-limits`,
  deny-all access, hidden from the admin nav).
- Extends your `users` collection with `roles` and `identities`
  fields (customize via `usersCollection` / `emailField` /
  `rolesField` / `identitiesField`), registers the `auth-link`
  strategy, and mounts `GET` + `DELETE /api/auth-link/session`.
- Validates everything fail-fast: bad secrets, unknown roles, or
  zero providers throw at config time, not on first login.

Users stay first-class Payload documents: the admin users list shows
roles and linked identities, and opening a row shows each identity
(`better-auth · user@example.com`). The `roles` / `defaultRole`
options above are the whole role vocabulary — Payload roles are the
single authority, and a provider's own role field (such as Better
Auth's `admin.role`) is never read: see [One role system: Payload
roles](concepts.md#one-role-system-payload-roles).

**Who creates users and who gets linked.** Collection-level `create`
on the users collection defaults to role-manager-only and `read` to
self + role managers (no user enumeration) — declare your own
`access` to change either. JIT linking attaches a verified provider
identity by email only to documents PROVEN to own that email (the
plugin's `linkable` marker, set automatically on plugin-managed and
manager creates); anything else is refused until an operator
resolves the collision — checks who created and owns the conflicting
document, then renames or removes it, or grants the proof only for a
document confirmed to be the address owner's own (Payload's
`_verified` is never proof, and neither is a fresh verification mail:
it proves the address, not the document). See
[concepts](concepts.md#one-role-system-payload-roles).

**Who edits roles.** The injected fields fail closed by default:
`roles`, `phone`, `suspendedUntil` and `suspendReason` are writable
only by the role-manager roles (`roleManagerRoles`, defaulting to
`['admin']` — required when you don't configure an `admin` role);
`suspendReason`, `suspendedUntil` and `identities` are readable only
by them; `identities` is engine-managed and read-only to everyone
else. A verified self-registered user can never grant themselves a
role. Your own access functions still win wherever you declare them
— the plugin only fills gaps. If your users collection carries other
fields users may edit, declare collection `access` explicitly; the
plugin does not guess a policy for fields it did not inject.

**Suspension and local credentials.** Suspension (`suspendedUntil`
in the future) refuses every session for that account — the provider
session, a local password sign-in, and any local JWT or API key the
account already holds (from the next request on it resolves no user:
every collection, file route, custom endpoint and `payload.auth()`
call sees an anonymous request). Documents with linked provider identities are
**provider-owned**: local sign-in, the forgot/reset-password flow and
Payload API keys are refused for them, and linking clears a key
enabled before it (`allowLocalCredentialsForLinkedDocs: true`
re-enables them during a migration window), while operator accounts
without linked identities keep local credentials and password
recovery. Roles listed in `policies.requireMfaForRoles` are withheld
from local-strategy sessions, which have no MFA proof. The full
matrix lives in [security-model.md](security-model.md).

## Edit 4 — Routes, middleware, UI

**Auth routes** (`app/api/auth/[...all]/route.ts`):

```ts
import { createRouteHandlers } from '@payload-auth-link/next'
import { auth } from '../../../../lib/auth'

export const { GET, POST } = createRouteHandlers((request) => auth.handler(request))
```

**Edge middleware** (`middleware.ts` + `lib/auth-cookie-names.ts`).
The middleware only checks cookie _presence_ (optimistic UX, never
authorization — real validation happens on Node). Cookie names come
from the dependency-free `/cookies` subpath so the Edge bundle never
imports server code:

```ts
// lib/auth-cookie-names.ts
import { getBetterAuthSessionCookieNames } from '@payload-auth-link/provider-better-auth/cookies'

export const exampleBaseURL = process.env.EXAMPLE_BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3100'
export const sessionCookieNames: readonly string[] = getBetterAuthSessionCookieNames({
  baseURL: exampleBaseURL,
})
```

```ts
// middleware.ts
import { createAuthMiddleware } from '@payload-auth-link/next'
import { sessionCookieNames } from './lib/auth-cookie-names'

export default createAuthMiddleware({
  sessionCookieNames,
  publicPaths: ['/', '/sign-in'],
})

export const config = {
  // Segment-anchored: bare `api`/`admin` prefixes would also exempt
  // frontend routes like `/admin-only` from the middleware.
  matcher: ['/((?!_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|api(?:/|$)|admin(?:/|$)).*)'],
}
```

Mounting Auth.js alongside (as `examples/basic` does — see the
[Auth.js guide](guide-authjs.md)) adds a second cookie-name source
and a second public sign-in path:

```ts
// lib/auth-cookie-names.ts (dual-provider delta)
import { getAuthJsSessionCookieNames } from '@payload-auth-link/provider-authjs/cookies'
import { getBetterAuthSessionCookieNames } from '@payload-auth-link/provider-better-auth/cookies'

export const exampleBaseURL = process.env.EXAMPLE_BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3100'
export const sessionCookieNames: readonly string[] = [
  ...getBetterAuthSessionCookieNames({ baseURL: exampleBaseURL }),
  ...getAuthJsSessionCookieNames({ baseURL: exampleBaseURL }),
]

// middleware.ts (dual-provider delta)
export default createAuthMiddleware({
  sessionCookieNames,
  publicPaths: ['/', '/sign-in', '/sign-in-authjs'],
})
```

**Server validation + hydration** (`lib/session.ts`, layout):

```ts
// lib/session.ts
import { createSessionVerifier } from '@payload-auth-link/next'
import { exampleBaseURL } from './auth-cookie-names'

// Anchor to the canonical origin: host headers are client-spoofable
// and the session cookie is forwarded to this origin, so the
// header-derived fallback is local-development only.
export const verifySession = createSessionVerifier({ baseUrl: exampleBaseURL })
```

`createSessionVerifier` options worth knowing:

- `baseUrl` — required unless `NODE_ENV` is exactly `'development'`
  (unset, `test`, `staging`, `preview`, and `production` all throw
  `InvalidConfigError` at construction). An absolute http(s)
  `sessionEndpoint` also satisfies it.
- `trustProxy` (default `false`) — development host fallback only:
  honor `X-Forwarded-Host`/`X-Forwarded-Proto`. Without it only the
  direct `Host` header is read, over `http`.
- `allowedDevelopmentHosts` (default: `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`,
  `[::1]`) — development host fallback only: any other host fails
  closed (`null`, reported via `onError`).
- `timeoutMs` (default `5000`) — the session fetch aborts after this;
  a timeout fails closed and is reported via `onError`.
- `sessionEndpoint` — a path starting with a single `/` or an
  absolute http(s) URL; protocol-relative values (`//host/x`) throw.

```tsx
// app/(frontend)/layout.tsx
import type { ReactNode } from 'react'
import { AuthLinkServerProvider } from '@payload-auth-link/next'
import { verifySession } from '../../lib/session'

export default function FrontendLayout({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>
        <AuthLinkServerProvider verify={verifySession}>{children}</AuthLinkServerProvider>
      </body>
    </html>
  )
}
```

**A sign-in form.** POST to Better Auth's endpoints, then refresh both
layers (`useAuthLinkRefresh` re-reads the session endpoint and
revalidates server state):

```tsx
'use client'

import { safeRedirectPath, useAuthLinkRefresh } from '@payload-auth-link/next'
import { useRouter, useSearchParams } from 'next/navigation'

const router = useRouter()
const searchParams = useSearchParams()
const refreshAuth = useAuthLinkRefresh()

const response = await fetch('/api/auth/sign-up/email', {
  method: 'POST',
  credentials: 'same-origin',
  headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ name: email, email, password }),
})
if (response.ok) {
  await refreshAuth()
  // The redirect param is attacker-controlled input: narrow it to an
  // in-app path so a crafted link cannot bounce fresh logins off-site.
  router.push(safeRedirectPath(searchParams.get('redirect')))
}
```

The example's full form (`app/(frontend)/sign-in/form.tsx`) adds
sign-in mode, error display, and the local-only dev verification
stamp — copy it.

## Run and verify

```bash
# Dev-only admin seed (explicit opt-in — nothing is seeded without it):
ALLOW_DEV_ADMIN_SEED=true DEV_ADMIN_PASSWORD=choose-a-password bun run dev:example
```

1. Open `/sign-in`, create an account — you land on `/account` with
   the `user` role.
2. `GET /api/auth-link/session` returns
   `{ user: { id, collection, email, roles } }`.
3. Open `/admin` (seeded admin: `dev@payload-auth-link.test` with
   your `DEV_ADMIN_PASSWORD`), browse Collections → Users: your user
   is there with its role and 1 linked identity.
4. Sign out via the user menu: the session is revoked, cookies are
   expired, `/account` bounces back to sign-in.

# Tour

A file-by-file walkthrough of `examples/basic` — the reference
integration every guide points back to, and the e2e target on all
three databases. Read this after [Getting started](getting-started.md)
to understand _why_ each piece exists.

Screenshots (regenerate with `bun run docs:media`):

![Home](media/01-home.png)
![Better Auth sign-in](media/02-sign-in.png)
![Auth.js sign-in](media/03-sign-in-authjs.png)
![Account](media/04-account.png)
![Admin users list with roles and linked identities](media/05-admin-users.png)

## Packages (what you install)

| Package                                   | Role                                                                                                                 | Imports                                                       |
| ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@payload-auth-link/core`                 | Domain: ports, `Role`, errors, wire contract. Framework-free — lint-proven zero framework imports.                   | `neverthrow`, `zod`                                           |
| `@payload-auth-link/plugin`               | Payload citizen: users extension, strategy, session endpoints, admin UI.                                             | `core`, `neverthrow`, `payload` (+ `react` peer for `admin/`) |
| `@payload-auth-link/react`                | Provider-agnostic UI: context, buttons, menu, role gates.                                                            | `core`, `react`                                               |
| `@payload-auth-link/web`                  | Framework-free web: route handlers, verifier, authz, redirect safety. No framework imports.                          | `core`                                                        |
| `@payload-auth-link/next`                 | Next adapter: Edge middleware, client refresh, server provider. Re-exports `web`. Only package importing `next/*`.   | `core`, `react`, `web`, `next`                                |
| `@payload-auth-link/tanstack-start`       | Start adapter: route handlers, request middleware, loaders, refresh. Re-exports `web`. Only package importing Start. | `core`, `react`, `web`, Start                                 |
| `@payload-auth-link/provider-better-auth` | Better Auth engine, Payload database adapter, port, collections.                                                     | `core`, `neverthrow`, `better-auth`, `payload`                |
| `@payload-auth-link/provider-authjs`      | Auth.js engine, Payload database adapter, credentials service, port, collections.                                    | `core`, `neverthrow`, `@auth/core`, `payload`                 |

Dependency rules (enforced by `no-restricted-imports`): `core`
imports nothing internal; UI packages never import Payload; React
never appears in the plugin outside `admin/`.

## The example, file by file

### `lib/auth.ts` — Better Auth engine

Creates the engine and re-exports the three things the rest of the
app needs: `auth` (the Better Auth instance for routes),
`betterAuthProvider` (for the plugin registry),
`betterAuthCollections` (for the Payload config). `loadPayload`
breaks the config ↔ engine import cycle with a cached dynamic
import.

### `lib/authjs.ts` — Auth.js engine (coexistence proof)

The same three exports for Auth.js: engine (JWT sessions, Credentials
provider wired to the credentials service), `handleAuthJsRequest`
for the catch-all route, `registerAuthJsUser` for the signup route.
Both providers live in one app to prove the registry design — most
sites pick one.

### `lib/auth-cookie-names.ts` — Edge-safe names

Computes both providers' session cookie names through the
dependency-free `/cookies` subpaths. The middleware imports this —
never the engines, which would drag `payload` and database code into
the Edge bundle and fail the build.

### `lib/session.ts` — Server verifier

`createSessionVerifier({ baseUrl })`, anchored to the configured
origin. The request-host fallback exists for local development only —
in production the origin must be explicit, because host headers are
client-spoofable and the session cookie is forwarded to that origin.
`EXAMPLE_BASE_URL` matches the running port in every mode, so the
example needs no per-mode configuration.

### `payload.config.ts` — Plugin wiring

SQLite file DB (switchable to Postgres/Mongo via `PAYLOAD_DB` for
parity runs), `users` + `pages` collections, both providers'
collections, the `authLink` plugin call, and an `onInit` seed for the
local admin. Provider users are never seeded — they provision
just-in-time at first session verification.

### `app/api/auth/[...all]/route.ts` — Better Auth routes

Mounts `auth.handler` with the uniform error envelope. All Better
Auth paths (`/sign-up/email`, `/sign-in/email`, `/sign-out`, …)
serve from here.

### `app/api/authjs/[...authjs]/route.ts` — Auth.js routes

Mounts the Auth.js engine's `handleRequest` at the engine's default
`/api/authjs` basePath — chosen to coexist with Better Auth's
`/api/auth`.

### `app/api/authjs-signup/route.ts` — Builder signup

Auth.js credentials store nothing themselves, so signup is an
explicit service call. This route wraps `registerAuthJsUser`,
answering new and already-registered emails identically (no
enumeration oracle; duplicates are an out-of-band notice) and
weak-password/bad-email → 400.
It stamps `emailVerified` immediately — **local example only** (no
email delivery); production builders verify out-of-band first.

### `middleware.ts` — Optimistic Edge check

Presence of any session cookie lets the request through; absence
redirects to `/sign-in?redirect=…`. UX only — route protection here
bounces obvious anonymous traffic early; authorization always happens
on Node (verifier, strategy) against live state.

### `app/(frontend)/layout.tsx` — Hydration

`AuthLinkServerProvider` validates the session on Node per request
and hydrates the client provider, so first paint already knows the
user — no loading flash, no client fetch waterfall.

### `app/(frontend)/sign-in/` — Better Auth form

Sign-in/sign-up modes POSTing JSON to `/api/auth/*`, then
`useAuthLinkRefresh()` + `router.push(safeRedirectPath(redirect))` —
the redirect param is attacker-controlled input, so it is narrowed to
an in-app path before navigation (open-redirect e2e asserts this).
Errors render in `role="alert"` (the e2e wrong-password spec asserts
this).

### `app/(frontend)/sign-in-authjs/` — Auth.js form

Same UX over a different protocol: signup via the builder route,
then CSRF token + form POST to `/api/authjs/callback/credentials`,
follow the 302, and read success/failure from the final URL (Auth.js
always redirects — see the [Auth.js guide](guide-authjs.md)).

### `app/(frontend)/account/page.tsx` — Session consumer

`useAuthLink()` for user/roles plus `UserMenu` (email + honest
sign-out: revokes server-side, navigates home only on success).
`data-testid` hooks serve the e2e specs.

### `app/(frontend)/admin-only/page.tsx` — Server-enforced roles

`requireRoles` on Node before anything renders: anonymous visitors
bounce to sign-in, non-admins hit `notFound()`, and only admins ever
receive the content (e2e asserts the secret is absent from denied
responses). `RequireRoles` is UI-hiding only — it must never gate
content, because server-rendered children ship in the RSC payload
regardless.

## `examples/tanstack-start` — Same app on Start

The TanStack example mirrors `basic` file for file on Payload v4;
only the framework surface differs (see the [TanStack Start
guide](guide-tanstack-start.md)):

- `src/lib/auth.ts` — engine with `tanstackStartCookies()` in the
  builder's own `options.plugins` (never `nextCookies()` here).
- `src/app/api.auth.$.ts`, `api.authjs.$.ts` — splat routes via
  `createServerRouteHandlers`.
- `src/start.ts` — `createAuthRequestMiddleware` (+ reinstalled
  CSRF middleware); `/_serverFn/` stays public or RPC breaks.
- `src/lib/session.ts` — shared verifier plus `getSessionUser` /
  `requireAdminUser` server functions.
- `src/app/_frontend.tsx` — `createSessionLoader` hydration into
  `AuthLinkProvider initialUser`.
- `src/app/_frontend/admin-only.tsx` — `beforeLoad` awaits the
  server-function gate; same `admin-denied` marker as Next's
  `not-found.tsx` so one e2e suite covers both.

## Test layout

- `packages/*/src/__tests__/` — unit + SQLite-memory integration
  next to the code (751 tests).
- `e2e/` — one Playwright suite against both examples: auth
  flows, session lifecycle, admin inspection, a11y, smoke (24
  specs × 3 databases × 2 frameworks, with the SQLite suites run
  in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit; `helpers.ts` holds the shared hydration and
  Payload-version locators).
- `e2e/run-{,tanstack-}mongo.mjs`,
  `playwright.{,tanstack-}{postgres,mongo}.config.ts` — parity
  harness: per-run databases, zero shared state.

<!-- docs/concepts.md -->

# Concepts

The mental model behind the packages. Read [Mission](MISSION.md) for
_why_; this is _how it fits together_.

## Hexagon: core ports, swappable adapters

`@payload-auth-link/core` owns the domain and the ports; everything
else is an adapter:

- **`IdentityProviderPort`** — the seam. `getSession(headers)` narrows
  whatever a provider knows into a `ProviderSession`
  (`sessionId`, `providerUserId`, `email`, `emailVerified`,
  `expiresAt`); `revokeSession(id)` undoes it. Better Auth and Auth.js
  each implement it; WorkOS/Clerk will later. The port never exposes
  provider SDKs to the plugin.
- **`ProviderRegistry`** — id → port map, explicit at the composition
  root. No discovery, no magic: `providers: [betterAuthProvider]`
  in the plugin options _is_ the registry contents.
- **`UserRepository`** — Payload users behind CRUD + identity-link
  lookup. The plugin implements it over the Local API.
- **`SessionPort`** — the bridge: ask each provider for a session,
  JIT-provision the Payload user, return a provider-agnostic
  `Session`. Implemented once in the plugin; providers never touch it.
- **Leaf ports** (`LoggerPort`, `ClockPort`, `IdPort`, `TracerPort`,
  `CookiePort`, `TransactionPort`) — injected everywhere time,
  randomness, logs, or cookies are needed, so tests control them.

```
providers ──IdentityProviderPort──▶ registry ──▶ SessionPort ◀── UserRepository
(Better Auth, Auth.js)                                  │              (Payload)
                                                        ▼
                                              strategy + endpoints
                                    (Payload + web + Next/Start + React)
```

## Users are Payload documents

There is exactly one user store: your Payload `users` collection.
The plugin extends it with `roles` and `identities` (slugs
configurable) and registers the `auth-link` strategy. Provider data
(hashes, tokens, OAuth accounts) lives in the provider's own
deny-all system collections (`ba-*`, `aj-*`) — never in `users`.

**Just-in-time linking.** Nothing provisions a Payload user at
provider signup. At the first session verification for an unknown
provider identity, the session service creates the user (default
role) and links the identity — idempotently, so no signup ordering
or race can strand a provider user without its document.

**Verification gating.** Linking requires a verified email. Better
Auth enforces it via `requireEmailVerification` (defaulted on by the
engine); Auth.js credentials carry a builder-stamped `emailVerified`
through a JWT claim. An unverified identity resolves to 401 at the
session endpoint — a provider session is not yet a Payload session.

## One role system: Payload roles

There is exactly one role authority: **the `roles` field on the
Payload user**. Provider role fields — notably Better Auth's
`admin` plugin, which adds a `role` column to its user table — are
ignored by design. Nothing in the plugin, the adapters, or the web
helpers ever reads them: `ProviderSession` carries no roles, and the
`roles` on every `Session` / `SessionUser` come only from the Payload
document. Granting someone the BA `admin` role grants them zero
Payload rights; removing their Payload `admin` role demotes them
even if the BA row still says `admin`. (BA's own admin endpoints may
consult the BA role before acting — for example to start an
impersonation — but that only gates the provider mechanic; the
resulting session still resolves to the target's Payload roles. If
you use those endpoints, keep the BA value set by hand for that
purpose; there is no sync in either direction, deliberately.)

**Where roles live.** You declare the vocabulary once in the plugin
options — `roles: ['admin', 'user']` plus a `defaultRole` that must
be one of them — validated fail-fast at config time as canonical
lowercase slugs (`parseRole` / the branded `Role` type in core). The
plugin injects a required, multi-select field with exactly those
options onto your users collection (name `roles`, remappable with
the `rolesField` option). JIT-provisioned users start with
`[defaultRole]`; after that you edit roles where you edit any
Payload data — the admin UI or the Local API. The field requires at
least one role, so an emptied array can't persist. Because the
session service reloads the Payload user fresh on every request, a
role change applies to the very next request on every provider and
session strategy — no re-login, no token refresh, no sync job.

**Who may be linked by email (the JIT-linking proof).** A verified
provider identity is attached by email only to a document PROVEN to
own that exact address: the plugin stores WHAT was proven
(`linkableEmail`, set automatically on plugin-managed and
role-manager creates, and updated by the provider-email resync) and
the `linkable` toggle. The proof holds only while the document's
email still equals `linkableEmail` — a self-service email change
invalidates it automatically (the change itself clears `linkable`,
`linkableEmail` and, on `auth.verify` hosts, Payload's `_verified`),
and the stranger's placeholder from a pre-created document never
matches. Payload's own `_verified` flag is never proof on its own:
Payload keeps it across email changes, so a verified document that
moved onto someone else's address would otherwise inherit their
identity. When a provider identity does link, Payload's local
sessions for that document are cleared — a local JWT issued before
the link dies on its next request. Email changes over REST on
documents with linked identities are role-manager-only (the
provider's own resync is unaffected), and self-service local
passwords on plugin-managed documents are stripped: one document
never holds two independently owned credentials. Documents created
outside the plugin — pre-upgrade rows, imports that skipped the
marker — are never JIT-linked until an operator resolves the
collision: after checking who created and owns the conflicting
document, renames or removes it, or grants the proof from a reviewed
list confirming the document is the address owner's own. Never from
`_verified` (which may predate an email change) and never from a
fresh verification mail alone: that proves who controls the address,
not who built the document — on a squatted document it would hand the
victim the squatter's document (see [upgrading](upgrading.md)). The migration runbook
sets both fields from provider-verified emails. Unproven documents
also cannot be created by end users: collection-level `create` on the
users collection defaults to role-manager-only, and collection-level
`read` defaults to self + role managers (no user enumeration), unless
the host declared those access functions itself. When the document
holds a local password too, every link logs a warning.

**Who may edit roles.** The injected `roles` field (and the
governance fields: `phone`, `suspendedUntil`, `suspendReason`) are
writable only by the **role-manager roles** — `roleManagerRoles`,
defaulting to `['admin']` and required at config time when no
`admin` role exists. Everyone else is denied at field level, so a
verified self-registered user can never grant themselves a role
(Payload's field-access default would otherwise allow any
authenticated user to write any field of any document). Users may
still read their own roles. `identities` is engine-managed: writes
are denied for every REST/admin caller, and reads are limited to
role managers. Payload's Local API with `overrideAccess` (which the
plugin's own engine paths use) is never restricted — this gates
REST and the admin panel only. The default admin-panel grant is the
role-manager roles too, not "any signed-in user"; declare your own
`access.admin` on the users collection to change it.

**How roles are consumed**, in enforcement order:

1. **Payload access control.** The `auth-link` strategy projects the
   session onto `req.user`, so your collection and field access
   functions read `req.user.roles` like any Payload-authenticated
   request. Plugin-owned authorization lives in
   `plugin/src/access.ts` (CSRF checks and the impersonation deny
   layer — the roles field denies create/update while an operator is
   impersonating and, on top of the role-manager rule, so an
   impersonated session can never become a role-escalation path).
2. **Server authorization** — `requireRoles` in
   `@payload-auth-link/web` (re-exported by the Next and Start
   adapters) verifies the live session and requires _every_ listed
   role, failing closed with `ForbiddenError`; see
   [Server authorization vs UI hiding](#server-authorization-vs-ui-hiding)
   below. `RequireRoles` / `useHasRoles` on the client are the same
   Payload roles, for hiding only.

**How capability policies layer on this** ([capabilities
guide](guide-capabilities.md)) — still by narrowing or scoping
Payload roles, never by importing a provider's:
`policies.requireMfaForRoles` treats a session without MFA
assurance as missing the listed Payload roles (projected out of the
session user, unknown assurance failing closed), and Payload-owned
organizations (decision D1) carry a role _per membership_, checked
by `requireOrgRole` alongside the global roles above. Provider-side
role stores (BA `admin.role`, organization-member roles) stay
storage-compatible data, never Payload authorization.

To make someone an admin: set `roles` on their Payload user. That
is the only step, on either provider.

## Session flow (read-time, no webhooks)

There are no webhooks and no background sync. Every read is live:

1. Request carries provider cookies.
2. The session service asks each registered provider in turn
   (`getSession`). Provider failures are logged and skipped — one
   provider down never breaks the others.
3. The first live session wins — precedence is the order of the
   `providers` array, so a browser signed in through two providers
   resolves to the first registered one. Expiry is checked against
   the injected clock with **no skew leeway**: a session expires
   exactly at `expiresAt`. Keep the plugin host and the provider's
   session store on synchronized clocks (NTP) — a hard requirement,
   since a leeway would accept sessions the provider already
   considers expired. A provider reporting an empty session id is a
   port-contract violation and resolves to 401, never a 500.
4. The linked Payload user is resolved (or JIT-provisioned), then
   reloaded fresh — role changes apply to the very next request.
5. The endpoint/strategy returns `{ user: { id, collection, email,
roles } }` (`SessionUser` — the versioned wire contract in
   `core/src/http.ts`).

The Payload strategy is read-only: it never refreshes provider state,
so login loops are impossible by construction. Failures at any step
resolve to anonymous (`{ user: null }` / 401), loudly logged (the default console logger; pass `nullLogger()` to mute).

## Two-layer validation (both frameworks)

- **Optimistic bounce** (`createAuthMiddleware` on Next.js,
  `createAuthRequestMiddleware` on TanStack Start) — cookie
  _presence_ check. Bounces obvious anonymous traffic to sign-in
  early. Cannot reach the database, so it never authorizes.
- **Node validation** (`createSessionVerifier` in
  `@payload-auth-link/web`, strategy, endpoints) — full
  verification against live provider + Payload state. This is the
  only authorization that counts. Both framework packages re-export
  it, so one import covers either.

Next hydrates via `AuthLinkServerProvider` (per-request Node
validation into the React context); Start hydrates via a root
`loader` (`createSessionLoader`) into `AuthLinkProvider
initialUser`. Either way the client never fetches on mount unless
unhydrated.

## Server authorization vs UI hiding

- **Enforcement** (`requireSessionUser`, `requireRoles` in
  `@payload-auth-link/web`, re-exported by the Next and Start
  adapters) runs on Node _before_ protected content renders or a
  protected mutation executes. Anonymous callers bounce (default:
  throw `SessionInvalidError`), role-missing callers are denied
  (default: throw `ForbiddenError`) — pass your framework's
  `redirect()` / `notFound()` as the handlers (thrown, not
  returned), or catch in route handlers and map to 401 / 403.
- **Hiding** (`RequireRoles`, `useHasRoles` in
  `@payload-auth-link/react`) only controls what renders in the
  browser. It must never gate content: server-rendered children ship
  in the RSC payload regardless. Use it for menus and buttons, never
  for secrets.

## Logout semantics

`DELETE /api/auth-link/session` (CSRF-guarded):

1. Verifies the session to learn which provider owns it.
2. Calls that provider's `revokeSession` (deletes database sessions;
   a documented no-op for stateless JWT sessions), then best-effort
   revokes every _other_ provider session the request presents —
   verification stops at the first match, so a second sign-in would
   otherwise outlive logout. Sweep failures are logged, never fatal;
   the 401 path sweeps too (a provider session can be live behind a
   failed verify).
3. Expires **all registered providers' session cookies** (`Max-Age=0`),
   even on the idempotent 401 path — logout never leaves a live
   cookie behind, whichever provider issued it. The clearing write
   carries each cookie's live attributes (`Secure`, `Domain`, `Path`)
   reported by the provider, so `__Secure-` and custom-domain cookies
   actually die; providers that predate that hook fall back to
   prefix-derived attributes.

## Errors

Expected failures travel as `Result<T, E>` values with coded errors
(`SESSION_INVALID`, `USER_EXISTS`, `PROVIDER_ERROR`, …); only
programmer errors (bad config, corrupt storage rows) throw. Web
adapters map codes to status codes; core never touches HTTP. Loud
failures over silent fallbacks, always — a corrupt Auth.js row
throws `AdapterMappingError` (Better Auth's schema fail-fast is
`UnsupportedSchemaError`); it never becomes a quiet login failure.

---

<!-- docs/guide-better-auth.md -->

# Better Auth guide

`@payload-auth-link/provider-better-auth`: Better Auth with Payload
as its database, behind `IdentityProviderPort`. This guide covers
what the engine adds and constrains; Better Auth's own docs cover
`BetterAuthOptions` in full.

## Engine

```ts
import { nextCookies } from 'better-auth/next-js'

const engine = createBetterAuthEngine({
  getPayload: loadPayload, // cached getPayload thunk
  slugs: { session: 'sessions' }, // optional per-model overrides
  depth: 0, // Payload read depth for the adapter (default 0)
  collectionsAccess: undefined, // deny-all by default
  options: {
    baseURL: 'https://app.example.com',
    secret: process.env.PAYLOAD_SECRET!,
    // Framework cookie plugin, declared by you exactly as Better Auth
    // documents: `nextCookies()` on Next.js, `tanstackStartCookies()`
    // on TanStack Start. The engine never touches this list.
    plugins: [nextCookies()],
    emailAndPassword: { enabled: true },
    // …the rest is yours: rateLimit, session, advanced…
  },
})

export const { auth, provider, collections } = engine
```

`auth` mounts at `/api/auth/[...all]`; `provider` registers with the
plugin; `collections` spreads into `payload.config.ts`. The return
type is inferred, so plugin endpoints and `$Infer` session types flow
through untouched.

## Secure defaults

- **Verification required.** When `emailAndPassword` is present but
  silent on `requireEmailVerification`, the engine sets it `true`.
  Opt out explicitly only when you mean it (the example does — no
  email delivery — and says so). Unverified users hold provider
  sessions the plugin refuses to link (401 at the session endpoint).
- **No plugin-list surgery.** Framework cookie plugins
  (`nextCookies()`, `tanstackStartCookies()`, …) are declared in
  your `options.plugins` exactly as Better Auth documents them;
  the engine passes the list through verbatim. There is no second
  engine-owned cookie API to misconfigure — see the [TanStack Start
  guide](guide-tanstack-start.md) for the Start spelling.
- **No `databaseHooks` needed.** The plugin provisions Payload users
  lazily at session verification, so there is no signup hook to
  keep in sync and no ordering that strands users.
- **Guarded two-factor step-up.** With `twoFactor()` installed, a
  second factor verified on an existing session shares the sign-in
  lockout (`twoFactor({ accountLockout })`, reserved before the code
  is checked, so concurrent attempts cannot outrun it), a factor
  enrolled or re-issued after a session was created never proves MFA
  for that session, an enrolled factor is read, re-issued or removed
  only from an MFA-proven session, and an emailed OTP is not MFA
  proof. Set `twoFactorOtpChannelIndependent: true` on the engine
  when your `otpOptions.sendOTP` delivers outside the email inbox
  (SMS). See
  [Two-factor and MFA policy](guide-capabilities.md#two-factor-and-mfa-policy-cap-6).

## Pass-through philosophy

`options` is Better Auth's options minus `database` (wired to
Payload here — it is omitted from the type, so passing it is a
compile error). Everything else — `plugins`, `rateLimit`,
`session`, `account`, `advanced` — passes through verbatim.

## Custom fields and plugin models

The adapter serves the five core models out of the box, and anything
else you declare. `additionalFields`, plugin-added core fields (the
organization plugin adds `session.activeOrganizationId`), and whole
plugin models (the organization plugin's `organization`, `member`,
`invitation`) all work the same way: declare them on the engine, and
matching Payload columns are generated while the adapter allowlists
exactly what you declared.

```ts
const engine = createBetterAuthEngine({
  getPayload: loadPayload,
  customFields: {
    user: [{ name: 'favoriteColor', type: 'text' }],
    session: [{ name: 'activeOrganizationId', type: 'text' }],
  },
  customModels: [
    {
      model: 'organization',
      fields: [
        { name: 'name', type: 'text', required: true },
        { name: 'slug', type: 'text', required: true, unique: true },
        { name: 'logo', type: 'text' },
        { name: 'metadata', type: 'text' },
      ],
    },
    // …member, invitation…
  ],
  options: {
    user: { additionalFields: { favoriteColor: { type: 'string' } } },
    plugins: [organization()],
    // …
  },
})
```

Field types map to Payload columns: `text`, `number`, `boolean`
(checkbox), `date`, `json`. Declarations are strict both directions
at startup: an undeclared schema field, a declared-but-absent name
(probably a typo), and an undeclared plugin model all throw
`UnsupportedSchemaError` naming the offender. Payload owns the row
timestamps — never declare `createdAt`/`updatedAt`. Custom models
get their own `ba-*` collections (override the slug per model) with
the same deny-all access and `baId` id column as core models.

- **Cookie cache is off unless you enable it.** When Better Auth's
  cookie cache is on, the port disables it per read
  (`disableCookieCache`, `disableRefresh`) — session reads are
  always live, never stale cache.

## Roles: the `admin` plugin's `role` is not Payload authorization

Payload roles are the one role system; the BA `admin` plugin's
`user.role` is **ignored by design** — see [One role system: Payload
roles](concepts.md#one-role-system-payload-roles). The plugin's
extra fields are ordinary storage as far as this adapter is
concerned: declare `user.role` / `banned` / `banReason` /
`banExpires` and `session.impersonatedBy` via `customFields` like
any other plugin fields, and BA's own admin endpoints may consult
the BA role. But nothing maps it into a session, a `SessionUser`, or
a Payload access decision — set Payload `roles` to grant rights,
and treat `banned` the same way (provider-side and optional, never
the authority). The same applies to the `organization` plugin's
member roles: storage-compatible, not Payload authorization.

## Cookie names (middleware + logout)

Session cookie names derive from your options through
`getBetterAuthSessionCookieNames` (the dependency-free `/cookies`
subpath — import it in Edge middleware, never the engine):

```ts
import { getBetterAuthSessionCookieNames } from '@payload-auth-link/provider-better-auth/cookies'

getBetterAuthSessionCookieNames({
  baseURL,
  advanced: options.advanced, // custom names must mirror here
  session: options.session, // cookie-cache shape must mirror here
})
```

It mirrors Better Auth's own getter exactly (the cookie-suite
drift test asserts parity against the real getter, option for
option). A mismatch fails closed — everyone bounces to
sign-in — never open. Logout expires every registered name with
its live attributes (`Secure`, `Domain`), so keep this call in
sync with `options`. `crossSubDomainCookies` is mirrored too:
the clearing writes carry the same `Domain` Better Auth wrote
(`crossSubDomainCookies.domain`, else the `baseURL` hostname), as
do chunks, multi-session cookies and the `__Secure-` / plain
counterparts. A clearing write without that `Domain` would miss the
cookie, and the browser would keep the cookie-cache `session_data`
that Better Auth's own `/get-session` keeps answering from until it
expires. One residual: a dynamic `baseURL` (`allowedHosts`) without
an explicit `crossSubDomainCookies.domain` resolves the domain per
request inside Better Auth — set the domain explicitly there.

**Production needs a canonical https `baseURL`.** Secure-cookie
names follow one rule shared by every provider: an explicit
`useSecureCookies` wins, then the configured origin (https →
secure), then `NODE_ENV=production`. The https origin is the
only input on which both SDKs and the session layer's origin
anchoring agree — without it, production falls back to
`NODE_ENV` detection.

## Sessions and revocation

### Session tokens stay out of page JavaScript

The session cookie is `HttpOnly` so script can never read it. Better
Auth's own HTTP JSON hands the same token back, though: `/get-session`
returns `session.token`, `/list-sessions` the token of every live
session, and sign-in / sign-up bodies the new `token`. With Better
Auth's `bearer()` plugin installed, that raw token is a working
`Authorization: Bearer` credential, so a single XSS could lift a
session from every device.

The engine therefore installs a redaction plugin by default
(security-model row 28). For HTTP requests it removes
`token` from every session-shaped object in any JSON body (the
`/get-session` session, every `/list-sessions` and
`/admin/list-user-sessions` entry — each keeps its `id`), and the
session token from every `{ token, user }` body (sign-in, sign-up,
and the `/two-factor/verify-*` answers, which echo the PRESENTED
session's token on a step-up). Server-side
`auth.api.*` calls are untouched — trusted code keeps the full shape.

- **Revoking one device** with the Better Auth client: pass the
  listed `id` where Better Auth expects the token —
  `authClient.revokeSession({ token: session.id })`. The engine
  resolves an `id` to its token server-side; Better Auth still
  checks that the session belongs to the caller. A raw token works
  as before.
- **Token hand-off protocols are left alone**: the multi-session
  plugin (`/multi-session/*` switches and revokes by token) and the
  one-time-token plugin (`/one-time-token/*`). Installing them hands
  tokens to the page by design.
- **Opting out**: the engine option `exposeSessionTokens: true`
  restores Better Auth's raw responses, for a client that truly
  needs the token from a body (a native app, say). Pair it with
  `bearer({ requireSignature: true })`, which refuses raw tokens as
  Bearer credentials.
- **Wiring warning**: when `bearer()` without `requireSignature` meets
  a surface that exposes raw tokens (`exposeSessionTokens: true`, or
  the multi-session plugin), the engine logs a warning through the
  `logger` you pass it.

The `bearer()` plugin's own `set-auth-token` response header is its
documented delivery channel and is unaffected: a deployment that
installs `bearer()` chooses to hand the signed token to client code.

### Revocation

Database sessions: the port reads via `auth.api.getSession` (no
hand-rolled anything) and revokes via the internal adapter's
`deleteSession`. Sign-out through `DELETE /api/auth-link/session`
revokes server-side _and_ expires cookies; direct
`/api/auth/sign-out` calls revoke provider-side only (the plugin
never sees them — prefer the plugin endpoint).

## Query semantics and sort collation

The Payload adapter answers Better Auth's queries with the same
results as Better Auth's reference `memoryAdapter` — every operator,
`null` handling, case-insensitive `eq`, numeric/date sorting, and
`limit`/`offset` pagination are pinned against it by a differential
test suite. The documented differences:

- **String sort collation belongs to your database.** `findMany`
  with `sortBy` on a text field orders by the database's collation:
  binary on SQLite and MongoDB (`A, B, a, b`), the column collation on
  Postgres. The memory adapter uses `localeCompare` (`a, A, b, B`).
  Payload exposes no portable collation option, and re-sorting in
  memory would break paginated windows, so the adapter does not
  normalise. Better Auth core never pages through string-sorted
  results; plugins or app code that do should sort on a normalised
  (e.g. lower-cased) column.
- **String range comparisons follow the same collation.** `lt`,
  `lte`, `gt`, `gte` on a text field compare in the database's
  collation too — binary on SQLite and MongoDB, the column collation
  on Postgres (where e.g. `'B' < 'a'` can be false under a
  locale-aware collation). The memory adapter compares JS strings
  (code units). Same-case ASCII strings agree everywhere; avoid
  string range filters over mixed-case or non-ASCII data, or compare
  on a normalised column.
- **`NULL` in negative filters keeps the row**, like the memory
  adapter: `ne` and `not_in` on a nullable column include rows where
  the column is `NULL` (SQL's `NOT IN` alone would drop them; the
  adapter adds the `IS NULL` branch).
- **Case-insensitive `eq` is Unicode-aware on every database.**
  SQLite's `LIKE` folds ASCII only, so the adapter narrows on the
  value's ASCII fragments and decides the match in JS
  (`toLowerCase`) — `ÄRGER` finds `ärger` on SQLite too.
- **`null` placement** in sorted results follows the database
  (first in ascending order on SQLite/MongoDB, last on Postgres).
- **Unsupported operators fail loud:** `contains`, `starts_with`,
  `ends_with`, case-insensitive `ne`/`in`/`not_in`, and a
  case-insensitive `eq` combined with `OR` throw
  `UnsupportedOperatorError` instead of returning wrong rows.

## Rate limiting (builder-owned)

Same rule as everywhere in this project: the library ships no
throttles, so abuse control is builder-owned. Better Auth paths use
Better Auth's own `rateLimit` option (passed through verbatim in
`options` — the examples enable it at a generous dev-scale ceiling);
the Auth.js authorize path and the builder signup route use the
reference throttle in `lib/rate-limit.ts` — see [Rate limiting in
the Auth.js guide](guide-authjs.md#rate-limiting-builder-owned) for
the pattern. Note Better Auth's default special rules (3
sign-ups/sign-ins per 10s per IP) apply on top of your `max`: the
examples raise those two paths via `customRules` because shared-IP
dev traffic would otherwise trip them constantly. Production
deployments tune ceilings down, resolve real client IPs, and back
them with shared storage.

## Troubleshooting

`UnsupportedSchemaError` names the offending field or model —
inspect the `ba-*` row and your plugin's schema ask.
`AdapterOperationError` wraps the storage `cause`. Both are loud by
design: fix the row, don't retry blindly.

---

<!-- docs/guide-authjs.md -->

# Auth.js guide

`@payload-auth-link/provider-authjs`: Auth.js (@auth/core) with
Payload as its database, behind `IdentityProviderPort`. Fully
local: no SaaS, no webhooks — sessions verify read-time through
Auth.js's own session action.

## Install

```bash
bun add @payload-auth-link/provider-authjs @auth/core
```

(`@auth/core` ships as a dependency of the provider, but you import
it yourself for providers like `Credentials` in the engine below, so
it is a direct dependency too — same rule as `better-auth` in
[getting-started](getting-started.md).)

## Engine

```ts
import Credentials from '@auth/core/providers/credentials'
import { createAuthJsCredentials, createAuthJsEngine } from '@payload-auth-link/provider-authjs'

const credentials = createAuthJsCredentials({ getPayload: loadPayload })

export const engine = createAuthJsEngine({
  getPayload: loadPayload,
  // Required in production: anchors the internal session read (the
  // session cookie is forwarded there) and derives secure-cookie names.
  // Falls back to AUTH_URL, then to request host headers (local dev only).
  baseURL: 'https://app.example.com',
  options: {
    secret: process.env.AUTH_SECRET!,
    session: { strategy: 'jwt', maxAge: 3600 },
    providers: [
      Credentials({
        credentials: {
          email: { label: 'Email', type: 'email' },
          password: { label: 'Password', type: 'password' },
        },
        authorize: (candidate) => credentials.authorize(candidate),
      }),
    ],
  },
})

export const { provider, collections, handleRequest } = engine
```

Mount `handleRequest` at `/api/authjs/[...authjs]` (the default
`basePath`, chosen to coexist with Better Auth's `/api/auth`),
spread `collections` (`aj-*`) into the Payload config, register
`provider` with the plugin.

Engine fail-fasts (all `InvalidConfigError`, all at wiring time):

- **Credentials requires explicit `session: { strategy: 'jwt' }`.**
  Auth.js rejects credentials + database sessions at config time
  with loud 500s (`UnsupportedStrategy`); the engine fails faster
  with the fix attached — including through factory-wrapped
  providers, which it inspects the same way Auth.js normalizes
  them (called with `{}`).
- **Secret required** via `options.secret` or `AUTH_SECRET` — a
  missing secret throws here instead of 500ing on first use.
- `basePath` defaults to `/api/authjs`, `trustHost` to `true`;
  builders override both. `true` is mandatory, not a choice: raw
  `@auth/core` answers every request with `UntrustedHost` unless it
  is truthy (framework adapters consult `AUTH_URL` for trust, but the
  raw `Auth()` this engine calls never does — core-side, the env var
  is inert; engine-side, `AUTH_URL` remains the `baseURL` fallback).
  Host strictness comes from origin anchoring instead:
  `handleRequest` rewrites the request origin to the configured
  `baseURL` before core sees it, so forwarded host headers cannot
  steer redirects or callback validation. Set `baseURL` to the
  canonical origin in production; without it, requests pass through
  on their arrival origin (local-dev convenience only).

## Credentials: builder-owned signup

Auth.js credentials store nothing — registration is an explicit
service call, and **verification is your signup policy**: the plugin
refuses to link unverified identities, so credentials users stay
locked out until you stamp them.

```ts
// app/api/your-signup/route.ts
const result = await credentials.register({
  email,
  password, // min 8 chars (floor; raise via minPasswordLength, never lower)
  name,
  emailVerified: new Date(), // ONLY after real verification (email link, admin approval…)
})
if (result.isErr()) {
  const error = result.error
  if (error instanceof UserExistsError) {
    // No enumeration oracle: answer exactly like a new signup, and tell
    // the address owner out-of-band ("someone tried to register").
    await notifyAccountOwner(email)
    return Response.json({ ok: true })
  }
  if (error instanceof WeakPasswordError || error instanceof InvalidEmailError) {
    return Response.json({ error: error.message }, { status: 400 })
  }
  return Response.json({ error: 'registration failed, try again later' }, { status: 500 })
}
return Response.json({ ok: true })
```

Registration flows through the core `registerWithStore` use-case over
an `aj-users` store and never throws: errors arrive as values
(`UserExistsError`, `WeakPasswordError` / `InvalidEmailError`,
`AdapterOperationError` with its cause kept server-side). Map
`UserExistsError` to the **same** response as success: a distinct
409 tells anyone probing the route which emails have accounts. The
examples do this through `lib/signup-response.ts` (unit-tested for
identical status and body).

Passwords hash with scrypt (random salt, constant-time verify);
Auth.js never sees them — `authorize` reads the `aj-users` row and
returns the user (or `null` for unknown email / wrong password;
corrupt rows throw `AdapterMappingError`, loudly). Unknown emails
and hashless rows burn a dummy scrypt verification, so response
timing reveals no account existence.

**Why a separate credential store, not Payload's password auth?**
Credentials live in the provider-owned `aj-users` collection rather
than the Payload users collection's native `password` field.
Provider secrets stay with the provider, just as Better Auth keeps
its own accounts table, and Payload users stay identity documents
that any provider can link to. The cost is a second credential
pipeline to maintain. Moving to Payload-native password auth would
be a breaking change and needs its own design pass. It is tracked as
an accepted risk (ARCH-5), not a commitment.

The example's signup route stamps every signup immediately **because
it has no email delivery** — mirroring Better Auth's
`requireEmailVerification: false`. Do not copy that stamp into
production.

## The credentials callback contract

@auth/core's credentials callback **always answers 302** — to your
`callbackUrl` on success (session cookie attached), to the Auth.js
error page with `?error=…` when `authorize` rejects. There is no JSON
mode (`json=true` is a next-auth v4 convention @auth/core ignores).
Drive it like the example form does:

1. `GET /api/authjs/csrf` → `{ csrfToken }` (sets the CSRF cookie).
2. `POST /api/authjs/callback/credentials` (form body: `csrfToken`,
   `email`, `password`, `callbackUrl`), follow the redirect.
3. Read the final URL: `error=` means rejected — show the form error.
4. On success the session cookie is jarred; `refreshAuth()` and go.

## Sessions, claims, revocation

### JWT post-logout replay window

**Credentials are JWT-only** (Auth.js never touches the adapter for
them): users come solely from `authorize`, sessions are encrypted
JWTs. A copied token replays until `maxAge` — there is no
server-side revocation for stateless JWTs, and no denylist is built
(see `docs/SPRINT.md` Accepted risks for the deliberate deferral).
Logout expires every registered cookie (even on the idempotent 401
path), which stops the browser presenting the token but does not
invalidate copies.

The mitigation is a short window: credentials deployments default
to `session.maxAge` of one hour (3600s) instead of Auth.js's thirty
days, unless you set `maxAge` explicitly. Lower it further for
sensitive deployments; the window is always exactly your `maxAge`.

- The engine chains your `callbacks` with the claims the port needs
  (subject + verification timestamp). Yours run first; the claims
  layer wins on its own keys; a `null` jwt return (forced logout)
  is respected.
- The session endpoint (`GET {basePath}/session`) returns an
  allowlisted shape on both strategies:
  `{ user: { name, email, image, id, emailVerified }, expires }` —
  Auth.js's default shape plus the port's two claims. A `session` callback of yours keeps
  every key it returns except the adapter session row fields
  (`sessionToken`, `userId`, `id`), which are always removed; add
  what the browser needs explicitly rather than relying on them.
  On database sessions the credential is also removed at any depth:
  every nested `sessionToken` key, and every string (object value or
  array item) containing the live session token, so a callback that
  nests the session it was given (`{ ...session, debug: { session } }`)
  cannot leak it. The rest of your result is sent in its JSON form
  (`Date`s as ISO strings); a cyclic result fails the session read
  with `SESSION_SHAPE_INVALID`, as `JSON.stringify` would.
- The port reads sessions through Auth.js's own session action
  (never a hand-rolled JWT decode) and needs a `host` header to
  build the internal request — the plugin endpoints pass live
  headers through, so this just works.
- JWTs over ~4k chunk across `name.0`, `name.1`, …; the port joins
  them and logout expires the listed slots (default `.0`–`.2`, ~12k
  of token — ours measure ~550 bytes). Raise `chunkSlots` on the
  engine (and mirror it in the middleware names) when custom claims
  push past that; only tokens beyond the raised slots need Auth.js's
  own signout action, which clears arbitrary chunks.

## OAuth / database sessions

Add OAuth providers to `providers` as usual; the Payload database
adapter serves users, accounts, sessions, verification tokens, and
authenticators (Auth.js ids live in `auId`; accounts carry a
composite `key` since Payload has no compound unique indexes).
Database sessions revoke server-side via `deleteSession`. Mixing
OAuth (database) with credentials in one engine is impossible —
Auth.js forbids it — so credentials deployments stay JWT while
OAuth-only deployments may choose either strategy.

### Trusting a provider's verified email

Auth.js creates every OAuth user with `emailVerified: null`, whatever
the identity provider asserts, so the plugin's verified-email gate
refuses to link them (401). If you trust specific providers to verify
emails correctly, allow-list them on the engine:

```ts
createAuthJsEngine({
  trustProviderEmailVerification: ['google', 'acme-oidc'],
  // …
})
```

For allow-listed providers only, a profile asserting
`email_verified === true` for the user's own email stamps
`emailVerified` through the adapter, so the user can link. Nothing is
stamped by default, when `email_verified` is false or absent, or for
providers outside the list. Never combine this with a trusted
provider's `allowDangerousEmailAccountLinking: true` — dangerous
linking attaches accounts by email alone, which would defeat the
verified-email gate; the engine fails fast on that combination.

## Cookie names (middleware + logout)

```ts
import { getAuthJsSessionCookieNames } from '@payload-auth-link/provider-authjs/cookies'

getAuthJsSessionCookieNames({ baseURL }) // + useSecureCookies / sessionTokenName / chunkSlots mirrors
```

Concatenate with your other providers' names for the middleware
presence check. Only session-indicating cookies are listed —
csrf/callback cookies exist pre-login and never count as a session.

**Production needs a canonical https `baseURL`.** Secure-cookie
names follow one rule shared by every provider: an explicit
`useSecureCookies` wins, then the configured origin (https →
secure), then `NODE_ENV=production`. The https origin is the
only input on which both SDKs and the session layer's origin
anchoring agree — without it, production falls back to
`NODE_ENV` detection, which matches Auth.js on https deployments
but fails closed (session detection misses) on http ones.
(`@auth/core` exposes no public cookie getter, so these names
mirror its internal `defaultCookies` rule instead of deriving
from it; the Auth.js e2e specs run real Auth.js cookies through
this derivation and would catch upstream drift.)

## Rate limiting (builder-owned)

The library ships no throttles — core has no storage primitive for
counters, so abuse control is builder-owned. Auth.js core itself
ships none either, which is why the examples carry a reference
pattern — copy it, then harden it:

- `lib/rate-limit.ts`: a minimal in-memory sliding-window limiter
  (`createRateLimiter`), a 429 + `Retry-After` responder, and a
  forwarded-IP client key. Deterministic unit tests included.
- The builder signup route throttles per email (10 per 10 minutes):
  legit signups use each address once, so abuse of one address can
  never lock out another. Proven by `e2e/rate-limit.spec.ts`, which
  asserts ten uniform 200s → 429 + `Retry-After`.
- The `/api/authjs/*` catch-all (the authorize path) throttles per
  client IP at a generous ceiling (100 per 10 minutes).
- Better Auth paths use Better Auth's own `rateLimit` option (see
  the [Better Auth guide](guide-better-auth.md)) — also configured
  in the examples.

In-memory state is dev-scale: it neither spans instances nor
survives restarts. Production deployments keep the pattern (per-key
windows, 429 + `Retry-After`) but back it with a shared store with
TTLs (Redis, Upstash, Postgres counters) and tune ceilings down to
real traffic. Skipping throttles entirely leaves signup, sign-in,
and authorize open to brute-force and enumeration pressure.

---

<!-- docs/guide-tanstack-start.md -->

# TanStack Start guide

`@payload-auth-link/tanstack-start`: the same auth behavior as
`@payload-auth-link/next`, on TanStack Start. The framework-free
pieces (`createSessionVerifier`, `requireRoles`,
`safeRedirectPath`, `createRouteHandlers`) live in
`@payload-auth-link/web` and are shared verbatim — the Start
package holds only Start imports, and re-exports the shared API so
one import covers both. Day-one target is **Payload v4**
(`@payloadcms/tanstack-start` exists only on the v4 line, beta).

Every snippet below is copied from `examples/tanstack-start`,
which the shared e2e suite exercises on SQLite, Postgres, and
Mongo — if a snippet and the example disagree, the example wins
(and please file an issue).

Prerequisites: Bun 1.4+, a Payload 4 + Start 1 app, React 19.
All packages are ESM-only.

## Install

```bash
bun add @payload-auth-link/core @payload-auth-link/plugin \
  @payload-auth-link/react @payload-auth-link/tanstack-start \
  @payload-auth-link/provider-better-auth
```

(`@payload-auth-link/web` arrives as a dependency — install it
directly only to import the shared API without a framework
adapter.)

## Engine: declare `tanstackStartCookies()`, not `nextCookies()`

```ts
import { tanstackStartCookies } from 'better-auth/tanstack-start'

export const engine = createBetterAuthEngine({
  getPayload: loadPayload,
  options: {
    baseURL: process.env.EXAMPLE_BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3200',
    secret: process.env.PAYLOAD_SECRET ?? 'local-dev-only-secret-32-chars-min!',
    // Start owns cookie I/O here (not Next.js): declare Better Auth's
    // Start cookie plugin in your own plugins list. The engine passes
    // it through verbatim and never appends framework plugins itself.
    plugins: [tanstackStartCookies()],
    emailAndPassword: { enabled: true, requireEmailVerification: false },
  },
})
```

Pick the framework you mount on — each cookie plugin reads its own
framework's cookie store. Auth.js needs nothing
(`handleRequest` is already Request/Response). The plugin call in
`payload.config.ts` is identical to Next (framework-free).

## Mount provider routes (`server.handlers`)

```ts
// src/app/api.auth.$.ts
import { createServerRouteHandlers } from '@payload-auth-link/tanstack-start'

export const Route = createFileRoute('/api/auth/$')({
  server: {
    handlers: createServerRouteHandlers((request) => auth.handler(request)),
  },
})
```

Same envelope as Next's `createRouteHandlers`. Handlers receive
`{ request }` context — `createServerRouteHandlers` adapts that to
the shared implementation. Mount Auth.js the same way at
`/api/authjs/$`.

## Request middleware (`src/start.ts`)

```ts
import { createAuthRequestMiddleware } from '@payload-auth-link/tanstack-start'

const authRequestMiddleware = createAuthRequestMiddleware({
  sessionCookieNames, // from the /cookies subpaths, as on Next
  publicPaths: [
    '/',
    '/sign-in',
    '/sign-in-authjs',
    '/favicon.ico',
    /^\/api(\/|$)/,
    /^\/admin(\/|$)/,
    // …client asset prefixes (`/@`, `/_build`, `/src/`, …)
    // (`/_serverFn/` needs no entry: the middleware exempts Start
    // RPC by default — a redirect there corrupts the
    // server-function protocol — and server functions authenticate
    // themselves via the shared verifier. Set
    // `bounceServerFunctions: true` to opt out.)
  ],
})

// Defining start.ts disables Start's automatic CSRF middleware —
// reinstall it explicitly for server functions.
const csrfMiddleware = createCsrfMiddleware({
  filter: (ctx) => ctx.handlerType === 'serverFn',
})

export const startInstance = createStart(() => ({
  requestMiddleware: [csrfMiddleware, authRequestMiddleware],
}))
```

Optimistic parity with Next: cookie _presence_ bounces obvious
anonymous traffic early; real validation is always the verifier.
Both middlewares share one framework-free bounce decision,
`decideAuthRedirect` from `@payload-auth-link/web` (bounce matrix
unit-tested there); the adapters only map its verdict onto their
response types.

## Session reads: server functions + shared verifier

```ts
// src/lib/session.ts
import {
  createSessionVerifier,
  getSessionUserFromRequest,
  requireRoles,
} from '@payload-auth-link/tanstack-start'
import { createServerFn } from '@tanstack/react-start'
import { getRequest } from '@tanstack/react-start/server'
import { exampleBaseURL } from './auth-base-url'

export const verifySession = createSessionVerifier({ baseUrl: exampleBaseURL })

export const getSessionUser = createServerFn({ method: 'GET' }).handler(() =>
  getSessionUserFromRequest(getRequest(), verifySession)
)
```

Anchor to the configured origin (`EXAMPLE_BASE_URL` matches the
running port in every mode) — host headers are client-spoofable
and the session cookie is forwarded to that origin. Export a
helper, not a prebuilt server function, so bundler transforms
never go stale.

## Hydration: root loader + `initialUser`

```tsx
// src/app/_frontend.tsx
// AuthLinkProvider is provider-agnostic UI: it comes from react, not
// from the Start adapter (which re-exports web, not react).
import { AuthLinkProvider } from '@payload-auth-link/react'
import { createSessionLoader } from '@payload-auth-link/tanstack-start'
import { createFileRoute, Outlet } from '@tanstack/react-router'
import { getSessionUser } from '../lib/session.js'

export const Route = createFileRoute('/_frontend')({
  loader: createSessionLoader(() => getSessionUser()),
  component: FrontendLayout,
})

function FrontendLayout() {
  const { initialUser } = Route.useLoaderData()
  return (
    <AuthLinkProvider initialUser={initialUser}>
      <main>
        <Outlet />
      </main>
    </AuthLinkProvider>
  )
}
```

First paint already knows the user — no loading flash, no client
fetch waterfall. After auth changes, `useAuthLinkRefreshStart()`
re-reads the session endpoint and calls `router.invalidate()`.

## Role enforcement: `beforeLoad` + a server-function gate

`beforeLoad` runs client-side on navigation too, where
`getRequest()` is out of scope — so the check lives in a server
function (SSR and RPC alike), and `beforeLoad` just awaits it:

```ts
export const requireAdminUser = createServerFn({ method: 'GET' }).handler(() =>
  requireRoles(getRequest().headers, verifySession, {
    roles: ['admin'],
    onAnonymous: () => {
      throw redirect({ to: '/sign-in', search: { redirect: '/admin-only' } })
    },
    onDenied: () => {
      throw notFound()
    },
  })
)
```

`redirect()` / `notFound()` produce the router's control-flow
signal — they must be **thrown**, not merely returned, or
execution falls through to `requireRoles`' default errors. Denied
callers never receive the content (e2e asserts the secret is
absent from denied responses, and both examples render the same
`admin-denied` marker so one suite covers both frameworks).

## Payload v4 notes (all hit building the example)

- `withPayload` callers must apply `rsc(pluginOptions.rsc)`, with
  `@vitejs/plugin-rsc` + `react-server-dom-webpack` installed —
  else SSR 500s.
- `devServerExternalPackages: ['ajv']` — ajv's CJS breaks under
  the RSC rewrite.
- v4 flips the Local API access default: builder code (seeds,
  scripts) must pass `overrideAccess: true`. Every shipped
  plugin/provider call already does.
- Run the real `payload generate:importmap` for admin components
  (the example commits the generated map).
- The v4 admin list renders as `grid`/`gridcell` (not
  `table`/`cell`); the v4 login adds a show-password toggle. The
  shared e2e suite locates both.

## Run and verify

```bash
cd examples/tanstack-start && bun run dev        # :3200
bun run e2e:tanstack                             # SQLite, 33 specs × 3 engines
bun run e2e:tanstack-postgres                    # per-run database
bun run e2e:tanstack-mongo                       # memory replset
```

## Next steps

- [Getting started](getting-started.md): the Next path — same
  calls, same behavior.
- [Concepts](concepts.md): ports, JIT linking, verification
  gating, two-layer validation on both frameworks.
- [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md): failure modes and fixes.
