0.5.0/0.5.1 without `linkableEmail`): set `linkableEmail = email` ONLY
where the email still matches the linked identity's email; treat
anything else as unproven (the admin users list shows which rows lack
the marker). Role managers can do it per user over REST; bulk
migrations via the Local API (see the migration runbook).

## 0.3.x → 0.5.0 (JIT-linking proof + users create/read defaults)

Two more fail-closed defaults on the users collection (see the
published advisory for the attack they close):

- **JIT linking requires proof of email ownership.** A verified
  provider identity is attached by email only to documents carrying
  the plugin's `linkable` marker (set automatically on
  plugin-managed and role-manager creates; role managers can toggle
  it) or, in that release, Payload's own verified flag (no longer
  proof since plugin 0.11.0). Documents created outside the plugin
  start unproven: their returning users are refused (401, with a
  logged reason) until the collision is resolved — the document
  renamed or removed, or the proof granted after a fresh
  verification of its current address (see "`_verified` is not
  linking proof" above). **Runbook note:** the payload-auth
  migration script marks imported users `linkable: true`.
- **Collection-level `create` defaults to role-manager-only** and
  **`read` to self + role managers** (no user enumeration) — both
  only where the host hasn't declared that access function itself.
  Hosts whose end users self-register through Payload REST/local
  forms (rather than through a provider) must declare
  `access: { create: ... }` or route registration through the
  provider.

Upgrade impact: default-behaviour change — non-managers can no
longer create users over REST or list other users; unproven
pre-existing documents are refused at JIT linking until marked.
Negative e2e specs cover the refusal, the proven/imported path, the
create block, and self-only listing on all six adapter/example
combos.

## 0.3.x → 0.4.0 (security default change)

The injected users-collection fields now fail closed
(security hardening). Previously, Payload's own defaults made every
authenticated user able to write every field of every user document —
including `roles`. The new default policy:

- **Writes** to `roles`, `phone`, `suspendedUntil`, `suspendReason`
  require the **role-manager roles** — the new `roleManagerRoles`
  option, defaulting to `['admin']`. If your configured `roles` have
  no `admin`, the plugin refuses to boot without an explicit
  `roleManagerRoles: [...]`. Editors holding a non-admin role must be
  named there or they lose the ability to edit roles in the admin
  panel.
- **Reads** of `suspendReason`, `suspendedUntil` and `identities` are
  role-manager only; `identities` writes are denied to REST and the
  admin panel entirely (the engine manages linking through the Local
  API, which is unaffected).
- The **admin panel** is no longer granted to "any signed-in user":
  the default grant is the role-manager roles. Declare
  `access: { admin: ... }` on your users collection to restore a
  wider policy — the plugin wraps your function with the
  impersonation deny and otherwise leaves it alone.
- Local-API writes (`overrideAccess`) — the plugin's engine paths and
  your own scripts — are never restricted by any of this.

If you depended on users editing their own profile fields, declare
those fields' access explicitly; the plugin never guesses a policy
for fields it did not inject. The negative behaviour is pinned by
`e2e/access.spec.ts` (non-admin escalation, admin-panel entry, field
stripping, manager writes) across all six adapter/example combos.

## 0.3.x → 0.4.0 (organization membership uniqueness)

The memberships collection gains a **compound unique index on
(user, organization)** (issue #21): two concurrent invite-accepts or
owner-bootstraps could previously both pass the check-then-insert and
land duplicate rows.

Upgrade impact:

- **Push mode (dev):** the new index is added on boot. Existing
  duplicate rows make the index build fail — dedupe first (keep the
  oldest row per `(user, organization)`), then boot.
- **Migrations mode:** generate the migration as usual; it must
  create the unique index AFTER your dedupe step. Creating a unique
  index over duplicates fails on SQLite and Postgres alike.
- Fresh installs are unaffected; the sequential duplicate checks
  remain (the index is the concurrency backstop, not the only guard).

Also in this line: `setEmail` now rewrites linked-identity rows that
carried the old address, so the admin view no longer shows a stale
identity email; `@payload-auth-link/next` exports
`checkAuthCookies(request, options)` — a composable form of the
optimistic middleware for apps that run their own `proxy.ts`
pipeline.

## 0.3.x → 0.4.0 (adopting existing roles fields; migration guide)

The plugin now **adopts** a compatible existing `roles` field on the
users collection instead of throwing: a Payload `select` with
`hasMany: true` whose options cover every configured role is taken
over — required-ness, the default, and the plugin's governed write
access are imposed; host options and labels survive. Incompatible
shapes fail at config time with the exact remediation, and
`rolesField: 'role'` remapping now works against an existing `role`
column. Coming from `payload-auth`? There is a runbook:
[migrating-from-payload-auth.md](migrating-from-payload-auth.md) — the
data move, the roles adoption, the `req.user` projection (it is the
session projection, not the full document), session/cookie policy,
and a script sketch.

Upgrade impact: config-time behavior — previously-throwing setups
with a compatible roles select now boot and adopt it; the adopted
field gains the role-manager write restriction (roleManagerRoles).

## 0.3.x → 0.4.0 (audible by default)

`authLink` now defaults to a **console logger** instead of a silent
one: session refusals (expired sessions, channels not admitted,
suspensions, provider errors, a session-shaped cookie that resolves
to nothing) and the impersonation audit print without
configuration. Consequences and opt-outs:

- To restore the old silence, pass `logger: nullLogger()` explicitly.
- Per-request "invalid session" residue (every logged-out page load
  hitting the session endpoint) logs at debug level, not warn —
  actionable refusals keep their warning, with reason, provider and
  channel.
- New `onAudit` option: a durable sink for impersonation audit
  events (called in addition to the logger). With an
  impersonation-capable provider, a silent logger and no `onAudit`,
  the plugin warns once at startup that audit events are dropped.

## 0.2.x → 0.3.0

Install-level changes — read before bumping:

- **`better-auth` and `@auth/core` moved from dependencies to
  peers.** The providers no longer install them for you. If you
  already import them (you almost certainly do — you configure the
  BA server or the Auth.js providers), add them explicitly:

  ```sh
  # Better Auth tree
  bun add better-auth@1.7          # validated band: >=1.7.6 <1.8.0
  # Auth.js tree
  bun add @auth/core@0.41          # validated band: >=0.41.0 <0.42.0
  ```

  Missing peers fail at install time with a clear "unmet peer" (npm)
  or auto-install-warn (bun) — not with a runtime module-not-found
  three frames deep. The narrow bands are the point: a fresh install
  can no longer resolve an upstream minor nobody validated. Widening
  is a compat patch away once the matrix proves the new version.

- **`payload` peers tightened to `^3.83.0 || 4.0.0-beta.0`.** 3.83.0
  is the bisected floor for the named-plugin and global-hook APIs the
  plugin uses; the v4 pin is the exact tested beta (no caret — v4
  canaries were silently inside the old range and broken).
- **Framework peers got honest floors:** `next` is now
  `^15.0.0 || ^16.0.0` (16 e2e-tested by the examples), and
  TanStack Start is `^1.140.2` (the first version with the
  `createMiddleware` types the adapter uses) with
  `@tanstack/react-router` `^1.170.0`.
- **Runtime version assertions** are live (see above). On a peer
  outside the band you get `UnsupportedVersionError` at boot —
  actionable, before any write.
- **Role-config safety:** removing a role from
  `authLink({ roles })` now stops granting it on the next session
  (stored values are filtered at read time), and the first boot
  after the change logs one aggregate warning naming the drifted
  values and affected user count. See the
  [role runbook](#changing-or-removing-roles) before trimming roles.

No database shape changes in this line: the collection snapshots are
byte-identical to 0.2.x (enforced by `bun run schema:check` from
here on — a PR that changes a shape must carry an `Upgrade impact:`
changeset section and an entry in this file, or CI fails).

## Rolling deploys and rollback (N and N−1)

The compatibility criterion, tested by the golden-DB suite on every
change: **the previous minor boots and serves core flows on the new
schema, and the new minor serves pre-migration rows.** Concretely,
during a rolling deploy or a rollback:

- 0.1.1 code on a 0.2.x database works — extra nullable columns are
  ignored, and old Auth.js token writes (`key` absent) are accepted
  by the nullable unique index. Rollback is data-safe.
- Caveat: an old pod cannot know fields it predates (e.g.
  `suspendedUntil`), so a suspended user keeps verifying on old pods
  until the rollout finishes. Finish rollouts promptly; that window
  is inherent to N/N−1.
- **Dev-push makes downgrades destructive** (Payload/drizzle prompts
  to delete the newer columns; accepting loses data, declining exits
  silently). Never roll back through a dev-push boot. Migrations
  mode boots old code read/write against the new schema safely
  (that is what the N−1 test proves).
- Schema changes follow expand → backfill → contract across two
  releases; a column that a previous minor cannot write against
  (NOT NULL without default, narrowed type) must never ship.

## Changing or removing roles

Roles are stored on user docs as plain slugs and validated for
**format** at the boundary, but grant only what the configured
`authLink({ roles })` allows (B11). When you remove or rename a
role, stored rows keep the old value until rewritten — so:

1. **Drain first.** Reassign every user holding the role to its
   replacement (admin panel or `payload.updateOne`) while the role
   is still configured.
2. **Then remove it** from `authLink({ roles })`.
3. **Boot and read the audit.** The first boot logs one aggregate
   warning — `N user doc(s) carry roles outside the configured set:
'editor' (2)` — if anything was missed. Sessions already stopped
   granting the removed role at that boot (reads filter it), and a
   user whose _only_ role was removed is denied a record entirely
   (never silently upgraded to the default role — same policy as
   corrupt roles).
4. Re-add the role to the config (temporarily) to drain properly if
   step 3 shows stragglers; clean rows keep the warning away on the
   next boot.

Renaming = add the new role, drain, remove the old one. The audit
runs on every boot (`onInit`) and costs one indexed query.

## Running production on migrations, not push

Dev-push (`push: true`) is for development: it makes destructive
choices interactively and makes downgrades lossy (above). Production
runs with `push: false` and explicit migrations:

1. Create the migration in your repo:

   ```sh
   payload.migrate:create   # or: bunx payload migrate:create
   ```

   Review the generated SQL before committing it. For the 0.1.1 →
   0.2.x move it must add `key` **nullable** (see above) and the
   optional governance columns — anything NOT NULL without a default
   is a bug in the migration, not in your database.

2. Run migrations as a deploy step, before new pods serve traffic:
   `payload.migrate` (or `bunx payload migrate`) in the release
   job. The expand→backfill→contract policy means migrations run
   cleanly while old-version pods still serve.
3. Keep the migration files in the repo — they are the record of
   how each release moves the database, and the artifact you attach
   to upgrade notes when you operate more than one environment.

The golden-DB tests (SQLite in `bun run check`; Postgres and Mongo
in the compat workflow) boot the previous release's seed under the
current code in both push and migrations modes, so a release that
would strand an upgraded database fails CI before it ships.

## 0.0.x → 0.1.0 (initial release)

First published line. No migration — but confirm before adopting:

- Packages are **ESM-only**. CJS `require()` of any entry (including
  `/cookies` subpaths) is unsupported; use ESM or dynamic import.
- The example's email-verification shortcuts
  (`requireEmailVerification: false`, immediate `emailVerified`
  stamps) are **local-dev-only**. Production must verify out-of-band.
- `payload.config.ts` collections for both providers are additive
  (`ba-*`, `aj-*`); the `users` extension adds `roles` +
  `identities` fields. No host migrations ship — your migration
  tooling owns schema changes (host-owned migrations only, per DNA).

## Session wire contract gains optional facts (PORT-4)

Additive only — no migration, and mixed versions keep working:

- **`SessionUser` and the plugin-level `Session` gain three optional
  fields**: `assurance` (`{ methods, mfa }`, how the session was
  proven), `actor` (`{ providerUserId }`, present only while an
  operator impersonates the user), and `organizationId` (the
  provider-native active tenant, when one is active). The session
  endpoint, the Payload auth strategy, the web verifier/`require*`
  helpers, and the React provider all carry them through.
- **Old payloads still parse.** A server that predates these fields
  simply omits them; clients see them as absent. Newer servers omit
  a field unless it is known — never `null`, never a fabricated
  default (a stray `null` for `actor`/`organizationId` is accepted
  and normalized to absent).
- **`'unknown'` assurance is data, not absence.** When the provider
  reported assurance but cannot tell the method or MFA state, the
  values serialize as `'unknown'`. Treat absent and `'unknown'`
  alike in policy: neither satisfies a requirement (fail closed) —
  but they stay distinguishable for diagnostics.
- **Malformed optional facts degrade, never nuke the user.** The
  client wire parser ignores unknown keys inside
  `assurance`/`actor` (forward compatibility with newer servers)
  and degrades a present-but-invalid optional
  fail-closed-for-policy (`assurance` to `'unknown'`,
  `actor`/`organizationId` to absent); core identity fields
  (`id`, `email`, `roles`) stay strict. An impersonation marker
  still cannot be laundered away server-side: authorization and
  audit use the plugin's own fail-closed extraction, where a
  present-but-malformed `actor` on `req.user` still denies and is
  audited as `actorKind: 'malformed-actor'`.

## Channel admission and impersonation completion (CAP-13a, CAP-8b)

- **`authLink({ admitChannels })` gates session channels.** It
  defaults to `['cookie']`: a live provider session presented on any
  other channel (`bearer`, `api-key`, `device`) is refused at
  verification with the typed `ChannelNotAdmittedError` (401),
  before any linking. Both shipped adapters report `cookie`, so
  existing behavior is unchanged. CSRF is unchanged too:
  state-changing endpoints still always require CSRF proof.
- **`Session.actor` and `SessionUser.actor` are now resolved.** The
  plugin looks the impersonating operator up by provider identity:
  a linked operator appears as
  `{ kind: 'payload-user', providerUserId, userId }` with the
  operator's Payload user id. An operator with no linked Payload
  user stays explicit: `{ kind: 'provider-only', providerUserId }`
  — fail-closed (the session still verifies and is audit-logged,
  but the provider id is never presented as a Payload id, and the
  unresolved state is logged as a warning). `parseSessionUser`
  accepts the legacy `{ providerUserId }` form and normalizes it to
  `provider-only`. `ProviderSession.actor` keeps the provider form.
- **Impersonated Payload operations are audited.** The plugin adds
  a `beforeOperation` hook to every collection and global that logs
  `impersonated operation` through `LoggerPort` with actor, target,
  operation, collection/global, and document id where named.
- **Impersonation is restricted by default (D5).** On the users
  collection the plugin now denies admin-panel access and writes to
  the roles field while an actor is present; reads are unaffected.
  For your own collections, `denyWhileImpersonating(ops?)` (plugin
  export) builds a matching `access` map — default denies `admin`,
  `create`, `update`, `delete`, and `unlock` while impersonating
  and allows reads — or gate on `isImpersonating(req)` inside your
  own access functions (fail-closed; `impersonationActorFromRequest`
  is for attribution only and returns `null` for a malformed actor
  that still denies).

## Hardening in the first release line (review backlog)

Behavior that tightened before first publish. Each change fails
closed, and none needs a data migration:

- **`authLink({ secret })` is deprecated and ignored.** Nothing in
  the plugin signs or encrypts: provider sessions are protected by
  the provider's own secret, and Payload auth by Payload's `secret`.
  The option stays optional so existing configs compile; delete it.
  `validateStartupConfig` (core) no longer accepts a `secret` key.
- **`safeRedirectPath` refuses sign-in and API destinations.** It
  falls back when the destination is the sign-in page (default
  `/sign-in`) or sits under `/api`. Pass
  `{ signInPath, apiPrefix }` to match custom mounts, or
  `{ signInPath: null }` where landing on sign-in is legitimate. It
  moved to core; `web`, `next` and `tanstack-start` re-export it
  unchanged.
- **`SignOutButton` narrows `redirectTo`** through
  `safeRedirectPath`. Off-origin and API destinations go to `/`.
- **`requireRoles` validates its role list first.** An invalid role
  (e.g. `'Admin'`) throws `InvalidRoleError`, and an empty list
  throws `InvalidConfigError`. Use `requireSessionUser` for "any
  signed-in user".
- **Wiring rejects illegal cookie attributes.** Provider session
  cookie names must be RFC 6265 tokens (checked at registration).
  Cookie `Domain`/`Path` values containing `;`, `,`, whitespace or
  control characters throw at serialization.
- **Auth.js `authorize` lowercases the email** exactly like
  registration, so `User@X.com` signs in. A corrupt stored
  `emailVerified` throws `AdapterMappingError`, and a gapped session
  chunk set is a failed read, never a joined token.
- **Clocks must be synchronized.** Session expiry has no skew
  leeway (see concepts).

## Future: WorkOS / Clerk adapters (post-v1)

Reserved registry ids, no packages yet. When they land they will be
new optional dependencies (`provider-workos`, `provider-clerk`)
following the same engine → port → collections shape — adopting one
is additive to the plugin options, never a rewrite.

---

<!-- docs/stability.md -->

# Stability and upgrade policy

> **Status: this policy takes effect when a package reaches 1.0.0.**
> Until then the [pre-1.0 practice](#today-pre-10) below applies.
> The packages version independently (for example plugin 0.11,
> core 0.7, web 0.3), and each package moves to this policy at its
> own 1.0.

This page defines what counts as the public contract, what each
semver level may change, how things are deprecated and removed, how
security fixes ship, and what each release has to document.

## Today (pre-1.0)

This is the current practice, the same one stated under "Pre-1.0
policy" in [upgrading.md](upgrading.md#pre-10-policy):

- **A minor may break.** Option shapes, exported types and internal
  ports can change in a `0.x` minor. Every such change ships a
  changeset, a CHANGELOG entry, and (when you need to do something) a
  section in [upgrading.md](upgrading.md) named after the release
  versions.
- **A patch fixes bugs.** Most security fixes ship as patches (for
  example 0.10.1 with advisory GHSA-hxgq-9pww-59j4). When the fix has
  to tighten a default, it can ship in a minor (0.4.0's security
  default change).
- **The wire contract is already the anchor.** `SessionUser`, the
  endpoint paths and cookie behavior change only with a migration
  note, and new wire fields are additive and optional
  ([PORT-4](upgrading.md#session-wire-contract-gains-optional-facts-port-4)).
- **Schema changes are already gated.** The schema-change rules
  ([below](#collection-schemas)) apply today. CI enforces them with
  `bun run schema:check` and runs the golden-DB N/N−1 suite.
- **Exported types are already snapshotted.** `bun run api:check`
  fails when the built `.d.ts` surface drifts from
  `snapshots/api/<pkg>.txt`. Before 1.0, that forces a reviewed
  changeset. After 1.0, it forces the right semver level.
- **Only the latest `0.x` release gets security fixes**
  ([SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md)).

## The public contract (from 1.0)

### 1. Wire contract

Anything a browser, a client bundle built against an older version,
or a separately deployed service can observe:

- **Routes** under Payload's API route:
  `GET`/`DELETE /auth-link/session`, and, when organizations are enabled,
  `GET`/`POST /auth-link/organizations`,
  `POST /auth-link/organizations/invite` and
  `POST /auth-link/organizations/accept`. Their methods, CSRF
  requirement (the `x-auth-link-csrf` header, exported as
  `csrfHeaderName`) and status codes are part of the contract.
- **Session endpoint bodies**: `200 { user: SessionUser }`,
  `200 { user: null, guest: { id, providerId, expiresAt } }` for an
  anonymous provider session, and `401`/`403` with `{ error }`;
  logout answers `200 { ok: true }`. The `SessionUser` shape is `id`,
  `collection`, `email` and `roles`, plus the optional `assurance`,
  `actor`, `organizationId` and `mfaRequired`. Adding an **optional**
  field is a minor change. Removing a field, renaming one, or making
  one required is a major change. Parsers (`parseSessionUser`) must
  keep ignoring unknown keys, so an older client can read a newer
  server.
- **Cookies.** The plugin mints no cookie of its own: session cookies
  belong to the provider. The contract covers which cookie names each
  adapter reads, re-presents and expires on logout (the
  `getBetterAuthSessionCookieNames` / `getAuthJsSessionCookieNames`
  helpers in the `/cookies` subpaths, including the `__Secure-` and
  `__Host-` prefix rules). If a change would sign users out or leave
  a cookie behind on logout, it is a major change.

### 2. Configuration

- `authLink(options)` (`AuthLinkPluginOptions`), the provider engine
  factories' options (`createBetterAuthEngine`, the Auth.js engine),
  and the adapter options (`createAuthMiddleware`,
  `createAuthRequestMiddleware`, `createSessionVerifier`, …).
- **Defaults are part of the contract.** Changing a default that
  loosens security, or that changes behavior for code that did not
  set the option, is a major change. The one exception is
  tightening a default to fix a vulnerability (see
  [Security fixes](#security-fixes)).

### 3. Exported API

- Every **package entry point** in a `package.json` `exports` map:
  `.` for every package, plus `@payload-auth-link/core/testing`,
  `@payload-auth-link/plugin/admin`,
  `@payload-auth-link/provider-better-auth/cookies` and
  `@payload-auth-link/provider-authjs/cookies`. Deep imports into
  `dist/` are not supported and not covered.
- **Core's public API is the explicit list in
  `packages/core/src/index.ts`.** That includes the port interfaces
  (`IdentityProviderPort`, `UserRepository`, `LoggerPort`, …) that
  third-party adapters implement. Adding a **required** member to a
  port is a major change. Adding an optional one is a minor change.
- **Typed errors** are contract by class (`instanceof`) and by the
  data they carry, not by message text.
- **`onAudit` events** are contract: the two messages
  (`impersonated operation`, `server session created`) and their
  field names ([audit.md](audit.md)). Audit consumers key on them.
- The API snapshot (`snapshots/api/`) is the mechanical check. A
  snapshot diff that removes or narrows anything needs a major
  changeset.
- **Not contract:** anything not reachable from an entry point;
  exports whose TSDoc says "Not public API" (for example
  `registerAuthLinkServer`); log message text and the fields of
  logger-only events; error message strings; the admin UI's markup;
  the example apps.

### 4. Collection schemas

The shapes Payload pushes or migrates are covered by the contract:
the provider collections (`ba-*`, `aj-*`), the organization
collections, and the fields the plugin injects into users. The
committed `snapshots/schema/*.json` is the mechanical check. These
are the rules from [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md), which apply before and
after 1.0:

- **Additive only by default.** A new column must be nullable or
  have a database default. Adding a column is a minor change, and
  the release notes must include migration steps.
- **No nullability, type or unique change, and no rename,** without
  a two-release expand → backfill → contract sequence. The previous
  minor must keep reading **and** writing the new schema. The golden-DB
  suite tests N against N−1.
- After 1.0, the **contract** step (dropping or narrowing what was
  expanded) is a major change.
- Every shape change ships a regenerated snapshot, a changeset with
  an `Upgrade impact:` section, an entry in `upgrading.md`, and a
  golden-DB upgrade test.

### 5. Supported bands

The runtime `supportedPayloadBand`, `supportedBetterAuthBand` and
`supportedAuthJsBand` constants equal the manifest peer ranges and
the CI compat matrix ([compatibility.md](compatibility.md)). They
always move together.

- **Widening** a band to an upstream version the matrix has proven
  is a patch or minor change.
- **Dropping** a supported upstream version, a database adapter or a
  Node major is a major change. The exception is an upstream that
  is itself end-of-life or has a vulnerability with no fix in that
  line. That exception ships with an advisory.

## Semver after 1.0

| Level | May contain                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ----- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| major | any breaking change to the contract above; removal of anything deprecated in an earlier minor; schema contract steps; dropped bands                                                                                |
| minor | new options, exports, endpoints, optional wire fields, optional port members; additive schema (nullable/defaulted, with a migration); deprecations (with warnings); widened bands; security tightening (see below) |
| patch | bug fixes that restore documented behavior; security fixes that keep the contract; widened bands; docs                                                                                                             |

A fix that makes the code match its documentation is a patch, even if
someone depended on the bug. If the documentation was wrong instead,
the docs are corrected and the behavior stays.

## Deprecation policy

1. **Announce in a minor.** The deprecated API gets a TSDoc
   `@deprecated` tag that names the replacement, a CHANGELOG entry,
   and an `upgrading.md` entry. Where it can be detected at runtime,
   it also logs **one** warning through the configured logger (the
   pattern the payload-auth compat shim already follows).
2. **Keep it working for at least one minor.** The deprecated path
   behaves as before for at least one minor release after the one
   that deprecated it.
3. **Remove only in a major.** Removal ships in the next major after
   that window, and the `upgrading.md` section for that major lists
   every removal.

Time-boxed compatibility windows that are documented as dated (for
example `legacySessions` for payload-auth cookies) end on their
documented date. That is not a breaking change.

## Security fixes

- **Report privately** through GitHub security advisories
  ([SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md)). Response targets are listed there.
- **Supported lines:** the latest minor of the current major.
  Proposed for 1.0: the last minor of the previous major also gets
  security patches for six months after a new major ships.
- **Delivery:** a patch release on each supported line, a published
  GitHub advisory (GHSA) with a CVE where one applies, and an
  `upgrading.md` entry when you need to do something.
- **Breaking for safety:** when the only safe fix changes the
  contract (tightening a default, refusing a credential path that
  used to work), the fix ships in a **minor** with the advisory and
  an `Upgrade impact` note that explains the opt-out, if one exists.
  It does not wait for the next major.

## Upgrade guide requirement

Every **minor** release, and any patch that needs operator action,
gets a section in [upgrading.md](upgrading.md):

- A heading that names the released version of every package that
  moved.
- What changed in behavior, what you have to do (configuration,
  migrations for each database adapter, cookie or session effects
  during a rolling deploy), and how to roll back
  ([N/N−1](upgrading.md#rolling-deploys-and-rollback-n-and-n1)).
- For schema changes, the `Upgrade impact:` section from the
  changeset (CI checks that it is there).

Every **major** additionally gets a single "x.y → (x+1).0" section
that lists every removal and every contract change.

---

<!-- docs/audit.md -->

# Audit trail for production

What the plugin records about security-relevant events, where those
records go, and how to keep them somewhere that survives log
rotation. Everything here is read off the code: `audit.ts`,
`server.ts`, `session.ts`, `collections.ts`, `lifecycle.ts`,
`organizations.ts`, `repository.ts`, and core's use cases. The
recipe at the end is tested in
`packages/plugin/src/__tests__/audit-sink-recipe.test.ts`.

## Two channels: `logger` and `onAudit`

The plugin writes everything through one `LoggerPort`
(`authLink({ logger })`). The default is `consoleLogger()`, so
refusals and audit events show up with no configuration: `info` goes
to `console.info`, `warn`/`error` to the matching console level,
fields render as a JSON suffix, and `debug` is silent. To mute all
output, pass `nullLogger()`. In production, pass an adapter for your
real logger (pino, OpenTelemetry logs and so on). `LoggerPort` is
`debug`/`info`/`warn`/`error(message, fields?)` plus
`child(bindings)`.

`authLink({ onAudit })` is a separate **durable sink**. Its type is
`(event: { message: string; fields: LogFields }) => void`. The type
is reachable as `NonNullable<AuthLinkPluginOptions['onAudit']>`;
`AuditSink` itself is not exported from the package root. The plugin
wraps the logger with `composeAuditLogger(logger, onAudit)`. On every
`info` call the wrapper first calls `logger.info(message, fields)`,
then `onAudit({ message, fields: fields ?? {} })`. `warn`, `error`
and `debug` pass through to the logger and never reach the sink.

**Only two events reach `onAudit`.** The composed logger is used
only by the impersonation audit hooks, the organization endpoints'
impersonation refusals, and `authLinkServer(payload).createSessionFor`.
Every other event in this guide reaches the logger only. To keep
those durably as well, wrap the logger (see
[Recipe](#recipe-an-append-only-audit-log-collection)).

When a provider can impersonate (Better Auth's admin plugin), the
logger is silent (`nullLogger()`) and no `onAudit` is set, the plugin
prints one `console.warn` at `onInit` saying that impersonation audit
events will be dropped.

## Events delivered to `onAudit`

### `impersonated operation`

Payload's `beforeOperation` hook does the auditing. The plugin adds
it to **every collection and every global** in your config, its own
included, after all hooks you defined. It also fires from the plugin's
organization endpoints: when they refuse a request because the caller
is impersonating, and for the organization list
(`GET /auth-link/organizations`, allowed while impersonating). And it
fires when verifying an impersonated session links the target's
provider identity to a users document, or provisions one
(`operation: 'linkIdentity'`) — a write no collection hook sees
under the impersonation. It is emitted only while an operator is
impersonating the request's user. Plain requests return before any
logging.

Because the hook runs `beforeOperation`, attempts that are later
denied are audited too. For example, a role change that is blocked
while impersonating still produces an event.

| Field                 | When present                                          | Value                                                                                      |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `actorKind`           | always                                                | `'payload-user'`, `'provider-only'`, or `'malformed-actor'`                                |
| `actorProviderUserId` | actor parsed                                          | operator's provider user id                                                                |
| `actorUserId`         | `actorKind: 'payload-user'`                           | operator's Payload user id (string)                                                        |
| `targetUserId`        | `req.user` has an id                                  | impersonated user's Payload id (string)                                                    |
| `operation`           | always                                                | Payload's operation name (`read`, `update`, `delete`, …), endpoint verb, or `linkIdentity` |
| `collection`          | collection hook, `linkIdentity`                       | collection slug                                                                            |
| `global`              | global hook                                           | global slug                                                                                |
| `endpoint`            | organization endpoint                                 | `/auth-link/organizations`, `/auth-link/organizations/invite`, `…/accept`                  |
| `denied`              | organization endpoint refusal                         | `true` (the endpoint answered 403); absent on the allowed list read                        |
| `id`                  | the operation args name a document id; `linkIdentity` | document id (string)                                                                       |

The fields carry ids only. Tokens, emails and document data are never
included. If the request carries an impersonation marker that cannot
be parsed, the plugin still audits it (fail-closed), with
`actorKind: 'malformed-actor'` and no made-up attribution.

For the organization endpoints, `operation` is `read`
(`GET /auth-link/organizations`), `create`
(`POST /auth-link/organizations`), `invite`, or `accept`.
Organization governance refusals that do **not** involve
impersonation (not a manager, role above your own, invitation not
yours) return 403 and are not logged.

### `server session created`

Emitted by `authLinkServer(payload).createSessionFor(userId, options)`
after the provider has stored the session.

| Field        | Value                                                                                                   |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `providerId` | provider that minted the session                                                                        |
| `userId`     | Payload user id (string)                                                                                |
| `sessionId`  | opaque session handle (the session row id, never the bearer token)                                      |
| `reason`     | the caller's required `reason` string                                                                   |
| `actor`      | the caller's optional `actor` string, when given                                                        |
| `mfaProof`   | the caller's `mfaProof` boolean, when given                                                             |
| `expiresAt`  | ISO timestamp of the expiry the provider **stored** (or the requested one if the provider reports none) |

`reason` and `actor` are free text you supply, so keep personal data
out of them.

## Events that reach the logger only

These are emitted through the configured `logger`, not `onAudit`.
The list covers the security-relevant ones (diagnostics such as
storage failures are left out). Message text is diagnostic output,
**not** a stable contract (see [stability.md](stability.md)). If you
key durable capture on these strings, pin them in a test of your own.

| Level | Message                                                                                                                 | Fields                                                                                                               |
| ----- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| info  | `impersonated session used`                                                                                             | `providerId`, `actorProviderUserId`, `actorKind`, `actorUserId?`, `targetProviderUserId`, `targetUserId`             |
| warn  | `impersonated session actor has no linked Payload user`                                                                 | `providerId`, `actorProviderUserId`, `targetUserId`                                                                  |
| warn  | `session refused: user suspended`                                                                                       | `providerId`, `userId`, `suspendedUntil`                                                                             |
| warn  | `<scope> verification failed: user suspended` (scope: `strategy`, `session endpoint`, …)                                | `suspendedUntil`                                                                                                     |
| info  | `suspend: provider sessions revoked` (one per linked identity when `suspendedUntil` moves)                              | `providerId`                                                                                                         |
| error | `suspend: provider session revoke failed`                                                                               | `providerId`, `cause`                                                                                                |
| warn  | `provider session channel not admitted` / `<scope> verification failed: channel not admitted`                           | `providerId`, `channel`                                                                                              |
| warn  | `sso session refused: email domain not verified for any organization`                                                   | `providerId`                                                                                                         |
| warn  | `provisioning refused: the email is held by an existing document that is not proven to own it`                          | `providerId`, **`email`**                                                                                            |
| warn  | `email link refused: …` (pre-existing document not linkable, or proof bound to another email)                           | **`email`**, `userId`                                                                                                |
| warn  | `link refused: provider email unverified` / `registration refused: provider email unverified`                           | **`email`**, `providerId`                                                                                            |
| warn  | `link refused: anonymous identity never links`, `link refused: session carries no email identity claim`                 | `providerId`                                                                                                         |
| info  | `identity linked`, `identity linked by verified phone`, `user registered via provider`                                  | `userId`, `providerId`                                                                                               |
| info  | `local sessions revoked on identity link`                                                                               | `userId`, `providerId`                                                                                               |
| warn  | `identity linked to a document that also holds a local password; …`                                                     | `userId`, `providerId`                                                                                               |
| info  | `email synced from provider`, `phone synced from provider`                                                              | `userId`, `providerId`                                                                                               |
| info  | `verified email synced onto the linked user` (provider `email-verified` event)                                          | `userId`, `providerId`                                                                                               |
| info  | `email changed outside the provider resync; linking proof reset`                                                        | `userId`                                                                                                             |
| warn  | `identity event ignored: unverified email change (D9)`                                                                  | `providerId`, …                                                                                                      |
| warn  | `local password reset refused: document holds linked identities`                                                        | `userId`, `operation`                                                                                                |
| warn  | `local credential refused at authentication` (GHSA-mjvh: a dead account's Payload local JWT / API key resolves no user) | `userId`, `strategy` (`local-jwt` / `api-key`), `reason` (`suspended` / `provider-owned` / `provider-owned-api-key`) |
| warn  | `membership relocation refused`, `membership user rewrite refused`                                                      | `membershipId`                                                                                                       |
| warn  | boot: `payload-auth-link: N user doc(s) carry roles outside the configured set: …` (stored-role drift, B11)             | (counts in the message)                                                                                              |

The **bold** fields are emails. Unlike the `onAudit` events, the
logger-only events are not all limited to ids. Treat your log
pipeline as holding personal data, or redact `email` in your logger
adapter.

Role changes have no dedicated event. A change made by an operator
while impersonating is captured by `impersonated operation`, and the
plugin's access rules refuse it. To audit every role change by
anyone, add your own `afterChange` hook on the users collection that
compares `previousDoc.roles` with `doc.roles`.

## Delivery semantics

- **Synchronous and in-band.** `onAudit` is called synchronously
  inside the audited code path: Payload's `beforeOperation` hook, the
  organization endpoint handler, or `createSessionFor`. The plugin
  does not buffer, batch, retry or deduplicate. Events arrive in call
  order, once per call.
- **The return value is ignored.** If your sink returns a promise,
  the plugin does not await it, and a rejection becomes an unhandled
  rejection. Start the write, then route its failure somewhere
  (the recipe below uses `.catch(onError)`).
- **A sink that throws is fail-closed.** A synchronous throw
  propagates. Inside `beforeOperation` it fails the operation the
  impersonating operator attempted (proven by the recipe test). In an
  organization endpoint, the refusal turns into an error response
  instead of the 403. In `createSessionFor`, the provider has
  **already stored** the session, but the call throws before
  returning the token, so the session stays orphaned until it expires
  or you revoke it with `revokeAllForUser`. Throw only if you mean
  "no audit, no action". Otherwise catch inside the sink.
- **The logger runs first.** If `logger.info` throws, the sink is not
  called for that event.
- **Cost on the request path.** Every operation performed while
  impersonating calls the sink. Keep the synchronous part cheap: an
  enqueue or a non-awaited insert.

## Recipe: an append-only audit-log collection

Keep the trail in Payload itself. Payload owns the users, so a
Payload collection keeps the audit records in the same database,
backups and access model. The collection is append-only: `create`,
`update` and `delete` are denied to everyone, and the sink writes
through the Local API with `overrideAccess: true`.

Do not pass `req` to the write. Without `req`, the row is written
outside the audited operation's transaction, so a denied or
rolled-back attempt stays recorded. The plugin's audit hook (which
runs on this collection too) then sees no impersonated user, so
writing an audit row never audits itself. If you passed the
impersonated `req`, every write would audit itself again,
indefinitely.

```ts
// lib/audit.ts
import { isRecord, type LoggerPort } from '@payload-auth-link/core'
import type { AuthLinkPluginOptions } from '@payload-auth-link/plugin'
import type { CollectionConfig, Payload } from 'payload'

type AuditSink = NonNullable<AuthLinkPluginOptions['onAudit']>
type AuditEvent = Parameters<AuditSink>[0]

const hasRole = (user: unknown, role: string): boolean =>
  isRecord(user) && Array.isArray(user.roles) && user.roles.includes(role)

/** Append-only audit trail: rows are written only through `overrideAccess`. */
export const auditLogCollection: CollectionConfig = {
  slug: 'audit-log',
  admin: {
    useAsTitle: 'message',
    defaultColumns: ['message', 'operation', 'actorUserId', 'targetUserId', 'createdAt'],
  },
  access: {
    read: ({ req }) => hasRole(req.user, 'admin'),
    create: () => false,
    update: () => false,
    delete: () => false,
  },
  fields: [
    { name: 'message', type: 'text', required: true, index: true },
    { name: 'operation', type: 'text', index: true },
    { name: 'actorUserId', type: 'text', index: true },
    { name: 'targetUserId', type: 'text', index: true },
    { name: 'fields', type: 'json', required: true },
  ],
}

/**
 * `onAudit` is called synchronously and its return value is ignored,
 * so the write is started here and never awaited by the plugin.
 * Every failure is routed to `onError` (never an unhandled rejection).
 */
export function createPayloadAuditSink(options: {
  readonly payload: () => Promise<Payload>
  readonly onError: (cause: unknown, event: AuditEvent) => void
}): AuditSink {
  return (event) => {
    const text = (key: string): string | undefined => {
      const value = event.fields[key]
      return typeof value === 'string' ? value : undefined
    }
    void options
      .payload()
      .then((payload) =>
        payload.create({
          collection: 'audit-log',
          // No `req`: the row is written outside the audited operation's
          // transaction (a denied or rolled-back attempt stays recorded),
          // and the audit hook on this collection sees no impersonated
          // user, so writing an audit row never audits itself.
          overrideAccess: true,
          data: {
            message: event.message,
            operation: text('operation'),
            actorUserId: text('actorUserId'),
            targetUserId: text('targetUserId') ?? text('userId'),
            fields: { ...event.fields },
          },
        })
      )
      .catch((cause: unknown) => {
        options.onError(cause, event)
      })
  }
}

/**
 * Optional: forward selected logger-only events (see the table in
 * docs/audit.md) to the same sink. Message text is diagnostics, not
 * contract, so pin the set in a test of your own.
 */
export function withDurableMessages(
  logger: LoggerPort,
  sink: AuditSink,
  messages: ReadonlySet<string>
): LoggerPort {
  const forward = (message: string, fields: AuditEvent['fields'] | undefined): void => {
    if (messages.has(message)) {
      sink({ message, fields: fields ?? {} })
    }
  }
  const wrapped: LoggerPort = {
    ...logger,
    info: (message, fields) => {
      logger.info(message, fields)
      forward(message, fields)
    },
    warn: (message, fields) => {
      logger.warn(message, fields)
      forward(message, fields)
    },
    child: () => wrapped,
  }
  return wrapped
}
```

Wire it in `payload.config.ts`. `getPayload` is called lazily, at the
first event, so referring to the config being built is safe:

```ts
import { authLink } from '@payload-auth-link/plugin'
import { buildConfig, getPayload } from 'payload'
import { auditLogCollection, createPayloadAuditSink, withDurableMessages } from './lib/audit'
import { appLogger } from './lib/logger' // your LoggerPort adapter

const auditSink = createPayloadAuditSink({
  payload: () => getPayload({ config }),
  onError: (cause, event) => {
    appLogger.error('audit write failed', { message: event.message, cause })
  },
})

const config = buildConfig({
  // …
  collections: [/* users, … */ auditLogCollection],
  plugins: [
    authLink({
      // …
      onAudit: auditSink,
      // Optional: also persist chosen logger-only events.
      logger: withDurableMessages(
        appLogger,
        auditSink,
        new Set(['impersonated session used', 'session refused: user suspended'])
      ),
    }),
  ],
})

export default config
```

Notes:

- `hasRole(req.user, 'admin')` checks the roles the plugin puts on
  `req.user`: canonical slugs by default, or stored values with
  `projectRolesAs: 'stored'`. Use whatever role your operators hold.
- Adding the collection is a schema change in **your** app. Create
  and commit a migration for it, as with any collection
  ([upgrading.md](upgrading.md#running-production-on-migrations-not-push)).
- Retention is up to you. Nothing prunes `audit-log`. Schedule a job
  that deletes rows older than your retention period, using
  `overrideAccess: true`.
- Do not include the two `onAudit` messages in the
  `withDurableMessages` set. They already reach the sink, and
  including them would write each event twice.

### Shipping to an external store instead

The same shape works for a SIEM or log store. The sink enqueues
synchronously and a background flusher ships the events (an HTTP
batch endpoint, a queue, OpenTelemetry logs). Keep the same rules:
never throw from the sink unless you want fail-closed behavior,
always catch failures of the async part, and keep the flusher's queue
bounded. If the store is unavailable, fall back to the logger rather
than dropping events silently.

---

<!-- docs/rate-limiting.md -->

# Rate limiting

**payload-auth-link ships no rate limiter, so abuse control is your
job.** Core has no shared counter storage, and a limiter that lives in
one process protects nothing once you run two. This guide lists
every HTTP surface the library exposes or relies on, gives a
starting limit and key for each, and says where to enforce it.

The numbers below are starting points for a typical app with a few
thousand users. Tune them against your real traffic. Every limit
should return `429`, with `Retry-After` when you control the
response.

## Where to enforce

| Layer                                                        | Use it for                                                           | Notes                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Reverse proxy / CDN / WAF (nginx `limit_req`, Cloudflare, …) | Coarse per-IP ceilings on every auth path; the first line of defense | Sees the real client IP; rejects traffic before your app spends anything on it                                         |
| Better Auth `rateLimit` (in the engine's `options`)          | Everything under Better Auth's base path (`/api/auth/*` by default)  | Built in, per IP + path, path-aware rules; needs shared storage in production ([below](#better-auth-built-in-limiter)) |
| Next middleware / Start request middleware                   | Payload's users auth routes, `/api/auth-link/*`, GraphQL             | Needs a shared store (Redis, Upstash, Postgres); see [examples](#middleware-examples)                                  |
| Route wrapper around a handler                               | Auth.js catch-all, your own signup route                             | Wrap the handler you pass to `createRouteHandlers` / `createServerRouteHandlers` (the reference examples do this)      |
| Payload `auth.maxLoginAttempts` / `lockTime`                 | Per-account lockout on local password login                          | Defaults are 5 attempts / 10 minutes. It is a lockout, not a rate limit ([pitfalls](#pitfalls))                        |

## Endpoint inventory

Paths assume Payload's default `routes.api` (`/api`), a users
collection with the slug `users`, Better Auth at `/api/auth`, and
Auth.js at `/api/authjs` (the provider's default `basePath`).

### Plugin endpoints (`/api/auth-link/*`)

Registered by `authLink()` (`endpoints.ts`; `organizations.ts` only
when `organizations` is configured). Each one verifies the session
itself, and every state-changing one also requires the CSRF proof.
None of them takes a password or a code, so these limits protect
cost (database reads), not credentials.

| Endpoint                                   | Purpose                            | Starting limit (key)            | Notes                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `GET /api/auth-link/session`               | current `SessionUser` (or guest)   | 300 / min (IP)                  | Called on page loads and by the client refresh hooks. Each call reads the provider session and reloads the user. Keep the limit generous: a 429 here looks like a sign-out to the UI |
| `DELETE /api/auth-link/session`            | logout (revokes provider sessions) | 30 / min (IP)                   | Anonymous calls are cheap (no provider walk)                                                                                                                                         |
| `GET /api/auth-link/organizations`         | caller's memberships               | 120 / min (IP)                  |                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `POST /api/auth-link/organizations`        | create an organization             | 10 / hour (IP); 10 / day (user) | Creates rows; also limit per signed-in user if orgs are self-service                                                                                                                 |
| `POST /api/auth-link/organizations/invite` | invite by email                    | 30 / hour (IP)                  | Each invite can trigger an email you send; cap it like any outbound-mail path                                                                                                        |
| `POST /api/auth-link/organizations/accept` | accept an invitation               | 30 / hour (IP)                  |                                                                                                                                                                                      |

The admin login view (`admin.loginView: 'provider'`) adds no endpoint
of its own. It posts to `${admin.authBase}/sign-in/email` (Better
Auth's route, see below), and Payload's own admin form posts to
`/api/users/login`.

### Payload's auth operations on the users collection

Payload 3 has no request-level rate limiter. These are Payload's
endpoints. The plugin adds hooks that refuse suspended and
provider-linked accounts, but it does not throttle them. A users
collection that the plugin creates disables the local strategy
(`disableLocalStrategy`), so local login and password reset are not
available there. A **host-owned** users collection that keeps
`auth: true` exposes all of them.

| Endpoint (REST)                                                  | GraphQL                            | Starting limit (key)                                      |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `POST /api/users/login`                                          | `loginUsers`                       | 10 / 10 min (IP) + `maxLoginAttempts` (account)           |
| `POST /api/users/forgot-password`                                | `forgotPasswordUsers`              | 5 / hour (IP); 3 / hour (email, if you can read the body) |
| `POST /api/users/reset-password`                                 | `resetPasswordUsers`               | 10 / hour (IP)                                            |
| `POST /api/users/verify/:token`                                  | `verifyEmailUsers`                 | 10 / hour (IP)                                            |
| `POST /api/users/unlock`                                         | `unlockUsers`                      | 10 / hour (IP); role managers only by default             |
| `POST /api/users/refresh-token`                                  | `refreshTokenUsers`                | 60 / hour (IP)                                            |
| `POST /api/users/first-register`                                 | —                                  | 5 / hour (IP); works only on an empty database            |
| `POST /api/users/logout`, `GET /api/users/me`, `GET /api/access` | `logoutUsers`, `meUsers`, `access` | general API ceiling                                       |

**GraphQL** carries every operation through one `POST /api/graphql`.
A path-based limiter cannot tell `loginUsers` apart from a harmless
query, and a single request can batch many operations. Do one of
these:

- If you do not use GraphQL, disable it (`graphQL: { disable: true }`,
  and in Next delete `app/(payload)/api/graphql/route.ts`).
- Otherwise, put a tight overall ceiling on `/api/graphql` (for
  example 60 / min per IP) and keep `maxLoginAttempts` on. It counts
  per account whichever transport the login came through.

### Better Auth (`/api/auth/*`)

Every Better Auth route is served by the engine's `auth.handler`
mounted on the catch-all, so Better Auth's own limiter sees them all.
The ones that matter for abuse (core plus the plugins the examples
enable):

| Route family                                                                                                                                        | Built-in default (per IP + path)           | Recommendation                                                                            |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/sign-in/*`, `/sign-up/*`, `/change-password`, `/change-email`                                                                                     | 3 / 10 s                                   | keep; it adds up to about 1,000/hour, so add a proxy ceiling for slow-and-steady stuffing |
| `/request-password-reset`, `/send-verification-email`, `/forget-password*`, `/email-otp/send-verification-otp`, `/email-otp/request-password-reset` | 3 / 60 s                                   | keep, or tighten to an hourly window (outbound mail)                                      |
| `/two-factor/*` (twoFactor plugin)                                                                                                                  | 3 / 10 s                                   | tighten verify routes, e.g. `/two-factor/verify-totp` 5 / 5 min                           |
| `/sign-in/magic-link`, `/magic-link/verify` (magicLink plugin)                                                                                      | 5 / 60 s (plugin `rateLimit` option)       | keep                                                                                      |
| `/sign-in/email-otp`, `/email-otp/verify-email`, `/email-otp/check-verification-otp` (emailOTP)                                                     | 3 / 60 s (plugin `rateLimit` option)       | keep; OTP guesses are the brute-force surface                                             |
| `/phone-number/*` (phoneNumber plugin)                                                                                                              | 10 / 60 s                                  | tighten send routes (SMS cost)                                                            |
| `/passkey/*` (`@better-auth/passkey`)                                                                                                               | global rule                                | `customRules` for `/passkey/verify-authentication`, e.g. 10 / min                         |
| everything else (`/get-session`, `/sign-out`, `/list-sessions`, `/api-key/*`, …)                                                                    | global `window`/`max` (default 100 / 10 s) | set a global `max` that fits your traffic                                                 |

Better Auth API keys (`@better-auth/api-key`) also have a separate
**per-key** limit, configured with the plugin's
`rateLimit: { enabled, timeWindow, maxRequests }` and stored on the
key row. That limit applies when a key is verified, which includes
`authLinkServer(payload).verifyApiKey`.

The limiter runs only on HTTP requests that pass through
`auth.handler`. Server-side `auth.api.*` calls are not counted, and
the plugin's own session reads use those calls. So
`/api/auth-link/session` traffic does not use up Better Auth limits,
and Better Auth's limiter does not protect it either.

### Auth.js (`/api/authjs/*`)

Auth.js core ships no limiter. Wrap the catch-all handler, as both
reference examples do (`app/api/authjs/[...authjs]/route.ts`,
`src/app/api.authjs.$.ts`):

| Route                                                                 | Starting limit (key)                                     |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `POST /api/authjs/callback/credentials`                               | 10 / 10 min (IP); also count failures per email          |
| `GET\|POST /api/authjs/callback/<email provider>` (magic link / code) | 3 / 10 min (email + IP), correct code included           |
| `POST /api/authjs/signin/<provider>` (starts OAuth / sends mail)      | 10 / 10 min (IP); mail-sending providers per email too   |
| `GET /api/authjs/callback/<oauth provider>`                           | 30 / 10 min (IP)                                         |
| `GET /api/authjs/session`, `/csrf`, `/providers`                      | general ceiling                                          |
| your credentials **signup** route (builder-owned)                     | 10 / 10 min (email); the examples' `authjs-signup` route |

The Auth.js engine reads sessions in-process (it calls `Auth()` with
a synthesized request), so the plugin's session checks never pass
through your wrapper.

## Better Auth built-in limiter

```ts
createBetterAuthEngine({
  // …
  options: {
    // …
    rateLimit: {
      enabled: true, // the default is "production only" (NODE_ENV)
      storage: 'database', // or 'secondary-storage', or customStorage
      window: 60,
      max: 300,
      customRules: {
        '/two-factor/verify-totp': { window: 300, max: 5 },
        '/passkey/verify-authentication': { window: 60, max: 10 },
        // false disables a rule; a function can decide per request
      },
    },
    advanced: {
      ipAddress: {
        // Pick ONE header your edge sets and clients cannot spoof...
        ipAddressHeaders: ['cf-connecting-ip'],
        // ...or walk X-Forwarded-For past your own proxies:
        // trustedProxies: ['10.0.0.0/24'],
      },
    },
  },
})
```

How the limiter behaves (Better Auth 1.7, read from its source):

- **Enabled** defaults to `NODE_ENV === 'production'`. Set it
  explicitly so staging behaves like production.
- **Key** is client IP + path. IPv6 addresses are grouped by
  `advanced.ipAddress.ipv6Subnet` (default `/64`). If no IP can be
  resolved, every client shares one bucket per path, and Better Auth
  logs a warning once. With `disableIpTracking: true`, requests
  without an IP are not limited at all.
- **Rule precedence**: built-in special rules, then plugin rules,
  then your `customRules`. `customRules` keys match the path exactly
  or with `*` wildcards.
- **Response**: `429` with an `X-Retry-After` header (in seconds), not
  `Retry-After`.
- **Storage**:
  - `memory` (the default) is per process, so it is wrong for more
    than one instance or a serverless deploy.
  - `database` uses the **`ba-rate-limits`** collection, which the
    provider always declares (`key` unique, `count`, `lastRequest`).
    There is no extra schema step. This adapter has no native atomic
    increment, so Better Auth uses its fallback: a snapshot-guarded
    update with retries. Under heavy contention on one key, that
    fallback can fail with a "could not complete an atomic increment"
    error instead of counting. Every limited request also adds
    database round trips.
  - `secondary-storage` uses your `secondaryStorage`, which must
    implement `increment`. This is the right choice at scale (Redis,
    Upstash). You can also supply `customStorage: { consume(key, rule) }`
    (atomic check-and-increment).

The reference examples enable the limiter with dev-scale ceilings
(100 sign-ins/min, because every e2e request shares one IP). Do not
copy those numbers to production.

## Middleware examples

Both examples count per IP in a shared store that you provide. The
interface below is yours to implement. One atomic `INCR` with
`EXPIRE` in Redis is enough:

```ts
// lib/rate-limit-rules.ts — framework-free, shared by both adapters
export type RateLimitStore = {
  /** Count one hit for `key` in a fixed `windowSeconds` window; resolve the new count. */
  readonly hit: (key: string, windowSeconds: number) => Promise<number>
}

type Rule = {
  readonly name: string
  readonly method: string
  readonly path: RegExp
  readonly windowSeconds: number
  readonly max: number
}

const rules: readonly Rule[] = [
  { name: 'login', method: 'POST', path: /^\/api\/users\/login$/, windowSeconds: 600, max: 10 },
  {
    name: 'forgot',
    method: 'POST',
    path: /^\/api\/users\/forgot-password$/,
    windowSeconds: 3600,
    max: 5,
  },
  {
    name: 'reset',
    method: 'POST',
    path: /^\/api\/users\/reset-password$/,
    windowSeconds: 3600,
    max: 10,
  },
  { name: 'verify', method: 'POST', path: /^\/api\/users\/verify\//, windowSeconds: 3600, max: 10 },
  {
    name: 'refresh',
    method: 'POST',
    path: /^\/api\/users\/refresh-token$/,
    windowSeconds: 3600,
    max: 60,
  },
  { name: 'graphql', method: 'POST', path: /^\/api\/graphql$/, windowSeconds: 60, max: 60 },
  {
    name: 'session',
    method: 'GET',
    path: /^\/api\/auth-link\/session$/,
    windowSeconds: 60,
    max: 300,
  },
  {
    name: 'org-create',
    method: 'POST',
    path: /^\/api\/auth-link\/organizations$/,
    windowSeconds: 3600,
    max: 10,
  },
  {
    name: 'org-invite',
    method: 'POST',
    path: /^\/api\/auth-link\/organizations\/invite$/,
    windowSeconds: 3600,
    max: 30,
  },
]

/**
 * The client IP, from ONE header your edge sets and overwrites
 * (Vercel: x-real-ip; Cloudflare: cf-connecting-ip). Never trust the
 * leftmost X-Forwarded-For entry — clients write it.
 */
function clientIp(request: Request): string {
  return request.headers.get('x-real-ip') ?? 'unknown'
}

/** A 429 to return, or null to let the request through. */
export async function rateLimit(store: RateLimitStore, request: Request): Promise<Response | null> {
  const { pathname } = new URL(request.url)
  const rule = rules.find((r) => r.method === request.method && r.path.test(pathname))
  if (rule === undefined) {
    return null
  }
  const count = await store.hit(`${rule.name}:${clientIp(request)}`, rule.windowSeconds)
  if (count <= rule.max) {
    return null
  }
  return Response.json(
    { error: 'too many requests' },
    { status: 429, headers: { 'Retry-After': String(rule.windowSeconds) } }
  )
}
```

**Next** (`middleware.ts`, or `proxy.ts` on Next 16). Compose the
limiter with the optimistic auth bounce using `checkAuthCookies`. The
matcher must include `/api` for the limiter to see those routes. The
reference matcher excludes it because the bounce must never run there:

```ts
import { checkAuthCookies } from '@payload-auth-link/next'
import { NextResponse, type NextRequest } from 'next/server'
import { sessionCookieNames } from './lib/auth-cookie-names'
import { rateLimit } from './lib/rate-limit-rules'
import { store } from './lib/rate-limit-store' // your Edge-compatible store (e.g. Upstash REST)

export default async function middleware(request: NextRequest): Promise<Response> {
  if (/^\/api(\/|$)/.test(request.nextUrl.pathname)) {
    return (await rateLimit(store, request)) ?? NextResponse.next()
  }
  if (/^\/admin(\/|$)/.test(request.nextUrl.pathname)) {
    return NextResponse.next()
  }
  return (
    checkAuthCookies(request, { sessionCookieNames, publicPaths: ['/', '/sign-in'] }) ??
    NextResponse.next()
  )
}

export const config = {
  matcher: ['/((?!_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico).*)'],
}
```

Edge middleware cannot import `payload` or database code (see
[troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md#edge-build-fails-importing-payload--database-code)),
so the store must be Edge-compatible, such as an HTTP Redis like
Upstash. If your store needs Node, wrap the Payload REST route
handlers in `app/(payload)/api/[...slug]/route.ts` instead.

**TanStack Start** (`src/start.ts`). Add a request middleware in
front of the existing ones. Returning a `Response` short-circuits the
request, the same way `createAuthRequestMiddleware` returns its
redirect:

```ts
import { createAuthRequestMiddleware } from '@payload-auth-link/tanstack-start'
import { createCsrfMiddleware, createMiddleware, createStart } from '@tanstack/react-start'
import { rateLimit } from './lib/rate-limit-rules'
import { store } from './lib/rate-limit-store'
import { sessionCookieNames } from './lib/session-cookie-names'

const rateLimitMiddleware = createMiddleware().server(async ({ request, next }) => {
  const limited = await rateLimit(store, request)
  return limited ?? next()
})

const authRequestMiddleware = createAuthRequestMiddleware({
  sessionCookieNames,
  publicPaths: ['/', '/sign-in', /^\/api(\/|$)/, /^\/admin(\/|$)/],
})

const csrfMiddleware = createCsrfMiddleware({
  filter: (ctx) => ctx.handlerType === 'serverFn',
})

export const startInstance = createStart(() => ({
  requestMiddleware: [rateLimitMiddleware, csrfMiddleware, authRequestMiddleware],
}))
```

**Route wrapper** (either framework), as in the examples' Auth.js
catch-all:

```ts
// Next: app/api/authjs/[...authjs]/route.ts
export const { GET, POST } = createRouteHandlers(async (request) => {
  return (await rateLimit(store, request)) ?? handleAuthJsRequest(request)
})
// Start: server: { handlers: createServerRouteHandlers(/* same function */) }
```

## Pitfalls

- **Spoofable client IPs.** Every client can set `X-Forwarded-For`,
  and any limiter that trusts its leftmost entry can be bypassed by
  rotating the header. Read one header that your edge overwrites, or
  walk the chain past known proxies (Better Auth's
  `trustedProxies`). The examples' `clientKey()` reads the first
  forwarded entry. That is a dev convenience, not a production
  design.
- **Shared IPs.** Offices, universities and carrier-grade NAT put
  many users behind one address, and IPv6 users get a whole `/64`. A
  tight per-IP limit there locks out real people. Keep per-IP
  ceilings generous, and put the tight limits on per-account or
  per-identifier keys (email + IP for OTP and magic-link callbacks,
  as the Auth.js examples do).
- **No IP at all.** Behind a proxy that forwards no client-IP header,
  every request lands in one bucket. Better Auth warns once. A
  homegrown limiter falls back to `'unknown'` and throttles everyone
  together. Fix the proxy rather than raising the limit.
- **`trustProxy` here is not about IPs.** The `trustProxy` flag on
  `createSessionVerifier`'s `hostPolicy` controls only the dev-mode
  origin fallback. Nothing in payload-auth-link resolves client IPs.
- **Lockout is a denial-of-service tool.** Payload's
  `maxLoginAttempts` locks the **account**, so anyone who knows an
  email can lock its owner out. Keep `lockTime` short, alert on
  lockouts, and stop the attacker with the per-IP limit first.
- **In-memory counters.** The examples' `lib/rate-limit.ts` and
  Better Auth's `memory` storage are per process. Behind several
  instances or on serverless, each instance counts separately, so
  the effective limit is the configured one times the number of
  instances.
- **The session endpoint is hot.** `GET /api/auth-link/session` runs
  on navigation and refresh. A tight limit makes signed-in users look
  signed out. Size it for page views, not for logins.
- **Body-keyed limits need care.** To key on the email in a login
  body, read `request.clone()` so the downstream handler still gets
  the body, and normalize the address (lowercase) before using it as
  a key.

---

<!-- docs/MISSION.md -->

# Mission

## Problem

`payload-auth/payload-auth` bolts Better Auth onto Payload CMS through
monkey-patches, stringly-typed schema maps, framework leaks, and `any`-heavy
plumbing. It fights Payload instead of extending it, so site builders inherit
its coupling, its silent fallbacks, and its upgrade risk.

## Mission

Build the enterprise-grade, strictly-typed, hexagonal replacement:
a Payload CMS v3 plugin that makes external identity providers
(Better Auth, Auth.js/NextAuth, WorkOS, Clerk) feel like first-class
Payload citizens — managed from Payload collections and the Payload admin —
while keeping every provider behind a swappable port.

## What "first-class Payload citizen" means

- Users live in a Payload collection. Roles, access control, hooks,
  validation, drafts, and versions behave exactly as in native Payload auth.
- Admins manage users, roles, and linked identities from the Payload
  admin — no second dashboard, no out-of-band user store. (Provider
  session mechanics stay with the provider; the `ba-*`/`aj-*` system
  collections are engine-managed and hidden from the admin nav.)
- The plugin follows Payload's plugin contract (`definePlugin`, strategies,
  endpoints, hooks, admin components, host-owned migrations) and never
  reaches around it.

## What "hexagonal" means here

- `core` owns the domain and the port interfaces; it imports no framework.
- Every external touchpoint — Payload storage, each identity provider,
  cookies/session transport, logging, tracing, transactions — is an adapter
  behind a port, registered explicitly at a composition root.
- Adding a provider means writing one adapter package, not touching the core.

## Provider roadmap

Initial build: Better Auth first, then Auth.js/NextAuth — the two
providers fully validatable with unit + e2e locally (self-hosted,
no SaaS dependency). Auth.js shipped after its research spike
(Phase 4): both adapters, integration tests, and e2e are green.

Deferred post-v1: WorkOS and Clerk. Both are SaaS-backed and cannot
be fully validated locally; their ports stay reserved in the design
(`IdentityProviderPort` + registry keyed by id) but no adapter
packages ship in the initial build.

No provider ships without its adapter, its integration tests, and its e2e
coverage.

## Non-goals

- No fork of, or compatibility layer for, `payload-auth` internals.
- No second user store, shadow session table, or out-of-band auth cookie.
- No framework code in `core`; no Payload imports in UI packages;
  no React in the plugin outside `admin/`.
- No `any` at module boundaries; no silent fallbacks; no `console.*`.

## Quality bar

Strict TypeScript, `neverthrow`-style `Result` errors at boundaries,
Zod-validated inputs, lint-enforced package boundaries, and mandatory e2e:
every auth flow (sign-in, callback, logout, session revoke, role-gated
access) is proven against a real Payload app in Playwright before
release. There are no webhooks by design — identity sync is read-time
via the plugin's session verification (docs/concepts.md).

---

<!-- docs/DNA.md -->

# DNA — engineering constitution

How this repo is built. Every decision below traces to the research
synthesis (D1–D18) or to `payload-onpage` precedent. Violating these
rules requires updating this file first.

## 1. Architecture: ports and adapters

- `core` owns the domain and all port interfaces (`core/src/ports.ts`).
  It imports nothing framework-specific — no `payload`, no `next/*`,
  no React, no provider SDK.
- Adapters live at the leaves: one package per surface.
- Wiring happens only at an explicit composition root
  (factory functions like `nextSession()`, `payloadRest()`).
  No DI container (awilix/tsyringe/inversify rejected: magic,
  weak inference, worse tree-shaking).
- Constructor injection everywhere: `RegisterUser(repo, ids, clock)`.
- Public API is the explicit export list in each `index.ts`.
  Exporting something new is a decision, not a side effect.

### Package map (mirrors payload-onpage)

- `@scope/core` — framework-free: ports, domain (roles, session
  types, errors), provider-neutral orchestration. Depends on nothing.
